Strains carry one of several forms of a DNA cassette that holds the resistance gene. The team typed cassettes from patients with MRSA in their blood. They compared the types with each patient's other illnesses.

Certain cassette types went with certain kinds of infection and illness. So the germ's genetic print gives clues about the patient and the disease course. That helps doctors tell apart strains picked up in hospitals from those found in the community. It also aids tracking of how MRSA spreads.
plos-pone-0009589:
Takayuki Teramoto and co-authors studied magnesium balance in a tiny worm in PLOS ONE in 2010. Magnesium is vital for cells, and its levels in the body must be held steady. In mammals, channels called TRPM6 and TRPM7 govern uptake in the gut and recovery in the kidney. The worm C. elegans has a related channel, GTL-2. The team tested what that channel does for the worm.

Worms that lack GTL-2 could not excrete magnesium properly. Excess magnesium built up as a result. So the same channel family solves the same mineral problem in a far simpler animal. The worm gives a handy model for the basics of magnesium control.
plos-pone-0010389:
Tamaryn Cashmore and colleagues tested a faster way to diagnose tuberculosis in PLOS ONE in 2010. TB is hard to confirm when a patient's sputum has few germs or none to spare. Standard culture takes weeks, delaying treatment. Blood tests that measure immune signals can detect TB, but need good samples. The team tried using induced sputum, coughed up with help, for a rapid immune test.

They checked both whether the approach was practical and whether it gave correct answers. A test that works on easier samples could speed care in busy clinics. It could also catch cases that smear tests miss. TB control depends on finding cases early, before spread. This study probes one shortcut toward that goal.
plos-pone-0010489:
Do Yeon Lee and co-workers found that boosting one stress pathway shields brain cells from amyloid in PLOS ONE in 2010. Alzheimer's disease features clumps of a protein fragment called amyloid beta. Those clumps trigger a cell defense program for misfolded proteins. One branch of that program runs through a sensor called PERK. The team activated PERK signaling and tested amyloid-stressed cells.

Turning the pathway up reduced the stress amyloid caused. A defense branch, tuned right, can protect rather than harm. That distinction matters because the same program is blamed in other settings for killing cells. Knowing which branch helps could guide Alzheimer's drug design. The study offers a specific protective lever inside a broad alarm system.
plos-pone-0010589:
Vivek Unni and colleagues filmed a Parkinson's-linked protein inside living mouse brains, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The protein, alpha-synuclein, builds up in the brains of people with Parkinson's disease. Earlier work relied mostly on dead tissue or cells in dishes.

Using imaging through a small window in the skull, the team tracked the protein in the cortex. Overall levels stayed steady over time. Still, the protein moved between cell compartments at different speeds. Seeing that movement in a living brain gives researchers a new way to test ideas about how the disease starts.
plos-pone-0010689:
Qiong-Ying Hu and colleagues pinpointed where the cat immunodeficiency virus grips its entry receptor, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Feline immunodeficiency virus infects cats much as HIV infects people. Both viruses enter cells through a receptor called CXCR4. A loop on the virus surface, named V3, does much of the gripping.

Earlier work had narrowed the key region to nine building blocks. New tests cut that region down further and named the exact spots that matter most. A precise map of the grip helps explain strain differences. It may also guide vaccines that teach cat immune systems to block that exact spot.
plos-pone-0010789:
Yoshitatsu Sei and colleagues tested how two genes tied to schizophrenia interact, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Neuregulin1 signaling through ErbB receptors is implicated in both schizophrenia and cancer. Two other genes, COMT and AKT1, each carry variants linked to schizophrenia risk. Whether they sway the same pathway together was untested.

In cell models, COMT and AKT1 jointly shaped the cells' response to neuregulin signals. Their combined effect was stronger than either alone, a pattern called epistasis. Cell migration driven by the pathway changed accordingly. Gene pairs that interact help explain why single-gene risk for mental illness looks weak: the risk may ride on combinations.
plos-pone-0010889:
Arjen van't Hof and Ilik Saccheri published this moth genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2010. The peppered moth is a textbook case of evolution in action: dark forms spread during the sooty industrial era, then faded as air cleaned up. Yet the gene behind the dark carbonaria form was still unknown, so the authors tested the obvious suspects.

They examined sixteen candidate genes, all previously tied to dark coloring in other insects, isolating and reading them in this moth. Then they checked whether versions of those genes traveled with the dark form in dozens of offspring from a cross between dark and typical parents. None of the candidates matched. Van't Hof and Saccheri rule out the usual suspects, narrowing the hunt for one of biology's most famous genes.
plos-pone-0010989:
Roberta Mason-Gamer, Melissa Burns and Marianna Naum published this grass phylogeny study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Elymus is a large genus of grasses related to wheat, and many of its species are allopolyploids, hybrids carrying full genome sets from two different ancestors. Untangling which ancestors contributed, and whether later crossing blurred the picture, has been difficult.

The authors sequenced parts of three unlinked nuclear genes from Eurasian and North American species carrying one genome set from Pseudoroegneria and one from Hordeum. Gene trees confirmed the hybrid origin, pointed to likely genome donors, and exposed cases where genes disagreed, signs of later introgression or of ancestral variation sorted unevenly. Mason-Gamer and colleagues show that a reticulate, net-like history, not a simple branching tree, describes these grasses, a pattern common in crop relatives.
plos-pone-0011089:
Falcone, Fazio, Lee and colleagues wrote a 2010 PLOS ONE study on teen mental health. They examined a protein called S100B in blood serum. The question was whether levels of this protein might signal suicidal thinking or behavior in adolescents, who are hard to assess with talk alone.

The team treated S100B as a possible early warning marker in young patients. A blood based signal, if it held up, could help clinicians act sooner. The authors present the idea as a lead that needs more testing, not a proven test. Even so, it opens a new route in the search for better risk tools.
plos-pone-0011189:
Squeri, Masia, Casadio and colleagues tested hand control in PLOS ONE in 2010. People had to track a moving target by hand while hidden forces pushed against their movement. The brain had to learn the force pattern and cancel it out to stay on target.

The study shows how the motor system compensates for unseen forces during tracking. That learning process is central to skills from tool use to sport. It also matters for rehab after stroke and for designing prosthetic limbs. Devices that work with this learning can feel more natural to their users.
plos-pone-0011289:
Nieto, Sadowy, De la Campa and colleagues studied a pneumonia germ's survival trick in PLOS ONE in 2010. Some bacteria carry toxin antitoxin systems that can halt their own growth under stress. The team tested the role of one such system in antibiotic tolerance in the pneumococcus, including in clinical isolates.

The system helped germs tolerate antibiotics rather than die, and it was conserved across patient strains. Tolerance differs from resistance but can still cause treatment failure. Drugs that disable the trick could make standard antibiotics work again. The finding aids the wider fight against hard to clear lung infections.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1289:
A memorandum by the United States Chiefs of Staff bears the date 18 July 1945. It joins the thick stack of staff papers from the summit's first days. The chiefs' office wrote at a pace that matched the talks themselves.

These papers were the staff mind in fixed form: facts weighed, options ranked, risks named. The envoys who bargained by day read them by night. This one is a single sheet in that stack, from the second day of the conference. Its place in the run is its meaning: steady, expert pressure behind the men at the table.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1389:
On 28 July 1945 Mikołajczyk wrote a fifth memorandum for the record of the Potsdam weeks. The Polish deputy prime minister's papers form the most personal run in this part of the volume. The text comes from the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official history series.

By the last days of July, the shape of the settlement was plain, and Mikołajczyk wrote against time. His memoranda speak to posterity as much as to the men at Potsdam. Since he could guess how little room he had to change their minds. Readers get the human scale of the conference here: one statesman, shut out of the room, filling pages while empires drew lines through his homeland.
frus-1945-50-intel-d89:
Russell wrote to Byrnes again two days later, on 20 April 1946. Two papers to the secretary in three days mark a question being closed. Foreign Relations of the United States prints it in the later volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

Quick follow-up papers usually carry decisions requested, answers supplied, or loose ends tied. In the State intelligence story, April 1946 tied many ends: staff, funds, and the office's place under the new central system. Readers should read the pair of Russell papers together, as the department's final word in this thread. After them, the volume's center of gravity shifts for good to the central group and its growing quarrels and duties.
frus-1945-50-intel-d189: "Central Intelligence Group Paper" bears the date 12 March 1947. It survives in print as document 189 of the State Department's Foreign Relations volume on intelligence, 1945 to 1950. The war had just ended, and the United States was keeping a central spy service in peace for the first time. The text belongs to the daily flow of paper that ran the early Cold War state.
frus-1945-50-intel-d289:
A memorandum dated 16 June 1948 links two senior offices. The sender was the Director of the Policy Planning Staff (Kennan). The reader was the Under Secretary of State (Lovett) and Secretary of State Marshall. The editors of Foreign Relations of the United States placed it as document 289 in the 1945 to 1950 intelligence volume. It was the CIA's first full year, and the Council was setting the rules for both open analysis and secret work.

The form is plain on purpose: a named sender, a named reader, and a short statement of the matter at hand. A reader can watch the system think on paper: a fact here, a doubt there, a choice asked for at the end. Pages like this one are the bricks of the story: plain, dated, and load-bearing.
frus-1945-50-intel-d389:
General Joseph T. McNarney addressed a memorandum to the Executive Secretary of the National Security Council (Souers) on 22 July 1949. The editors of Foreign Relations of the United States placed it as document 389 in the 1945 to 1950 intelligence volume. The Dulles Report had landed in January 1949, and Washington was arguing over which of its fixes the CIA should adopt.

The form is plain on purpose: a named sender, a named reader, and a short statement of the matter at hand. That plainness lets a reader see how an issue moved from a working office up to the men who decided it. Its worth lies in the trail it leaves: a dated, signed step in the long build-up of the CIA and the Council.
frus-1861-d89:
On 4 October 1861, Charles Francis Adams sent a further dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The dispatch is document 89 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

October opened the season when Southern agents grew bold in British ports. Adams watched for ships and guns bought with Confederate gold. His early October report belongs to that quiet counter work, done with notes and calls rather than arms. Adams used consuls in the ports as his eyes in the hunt for Southern ships. Eyes in the ports were the first line of a blockade that began on land.
frus-1861-d189:
Writing on 30 April 1861, William H. Seward addressed Mr. Stockton in a broad sweep of spring orders. The letter is document 189 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Stockton, like King the day before, gets no post in the record heading. Seward's end of April letters went out in a broad sweep of appointments and orders. This one shows the Secretary filling the ranks of the service as the war took hold. A broad sweep of spring orders reached posts from London to the smallest court. A sweep of that breadth left no post to guess at the new chief's mind.
frus-1861-d289:
A dispatch dated 29 May 1861 carried word from Mr. Morgan to William H. Seward in Washington. Congress received it as Document 289 in the papers printed with the President's message that year. The letter comes from the opening months of the Civil War, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

Readers get the field report side of the exchange, sent home for Seward to weigh and answer. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d89:
Washington's orders went out to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London in a dispatch dated 30 June 1862. Congress received it as Document 89 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. By then, in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d189:
On 14 November 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward sent a dispatch to Charles Francis Adams in London, printed as Document 189 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Adams was then in his second year as American minister to Britain.

That week the British cabinet formally set aside the idea of acting with France on the war. The choice removed the sharpest foreign threat the Union faced that year. Seward's letter of 14 November was written before the news could reach him. Part of the long effort that had helped bring the safer outcome about. No working cable crossed the Atlantic in 1862, so every answer waited on a mail steamer.
frus-1862-d289:
Document 289 is the second Seward dispatch to William L. Dayton dated 20 June 1862, printed in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Secretary of State William H. Seward sent both letters to Paris in the same mail.

Same-day pairs let the Secretary divide orders from information, so the envoy could act on one and file the other. The practice also doubled the paper trail, which is why single weeks in this file can look crowded. For the Paris story, the 20 June pair marks the calm desk work done just before the war's summer crisis. The Paris mail sailed from Le Havre and took about two weeks to reach Washington.
frus-1862-d389:
Simon Cameron wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 19 August 1862, in a report printed as Document 389 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Cameron was the American minister in Russia.

Cameron's August report traveled from St. Petersburg as the Virginia campaign moved toward its climax. News and envoy moved at the same slow pace, both overtaken by events. For the reader, the Russian letters of this month are a study in distance. A friendly post, faithfully kept, reporting on a war an ocean and a continent away. Russian goodwill gave Washington one capital where it need not argue its right to exist.
frus-1862-d489:
James Shepherd Pike reported from The Hague to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 19 March 1862. The dispatch is Document 489 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the year's official record.

Pike's reports mixed court business with the talk of Dutch merchants and editors, whose trade suffered when American commerce suffered. In March 1862 he wrote as the war's naval side widened and the ironclad news crossed the ocean. His letters home gave Seward a reading of Dutch feeling that was generally fair to the Union. For the reader, the Hague file shows how much a working minister's weekly judgment mattered. It mattered to a government fighting a war three thousand miles from its sources of news.
frus-1862-d589:
Thomas Corwin sent this report from Mexico to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 20 May 1862, though the volume prints it after Seward's later instruction. It is Document 589 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Corwin's May report belongs to the weeks after Puebla, when Mexican hopes rose and French plans hardened. From the capital he could describe both the government's resolve and its poverty. His letters kept Washington honest about what sympathy alone could not do. The slight disorder of the printed file, reports and answers interleaved out of date, mirrors the real delays of the correspondence itself. Read by date, Corwin's May letter answers a Mexico transformed by battle.
frus-1862-d689: On 5 March 1862, a Mr. De Long wrote again to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The dispatch is document 689 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862, the third of his letters in a span of two weeks. The evidence for it gives the writer, the date, and its place in the volume, but no post or topic.
frus-1863p1-d89:
Charles Francis Adams wrote this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 20 February 1863. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 89 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863, a lone sheet after a three-letter day.

A single letter after a flood often tidied a loose end or sent a late piece of news. Adams's February mail kept Washington wise to a court whose mood could shift with each debate. This dispatch is a quiet piece of that watch. It holds its place in the run, between the clusters of mid-February and the fresh orders soon to come from Washington.
frus-1863p1-d189:
The mail from London dated 7 May 1863 brought Secretary of State William H. Seward this report from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It stands as document 189 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress. It was one of 4 letters between the same men dated that day.

Confederate agents were busy in Britain buying ships, arms, and supplies. Reports from the London legation fed Washington's protests against that trade. For a modern reader, it offers the war as working diplomats saw it: slow mail, sharp words, and constant risk.
frus-1863p1-d289:
An instruction dated 10 September 1863 went from Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, in London. It appears as document 289 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

In the fall of 1863 two ironclad rams built for the Confederacy waited in a British yard. Washington's orders to Adams that season pressed hard for the ships to be held. It belongs to the tense autumn when the fate of two Confederate ironclad rams in British yards hung in the balance. It is a small piece of a huge correspondence, but the whole picture only emerges from pieces like this one.
frus-1863p1-d389:
To Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this formal note on 10 February 1863. It appears as document 389 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It is one of the papers the State Department later printed in its Foreign Relations series for 1863.

Trade bound the countries tightly, from Southern cotton to British mills. Both sides had much to lose from a break, and the notes reflect that caution. For a modern reader, it offers the war as working diplomats saw it: slow mail, sharp words, and constant risk.
frus-1863p1-d489:
From Secretary of State William H. Seward to Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons: a letter dated 4 May 1863. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message. The letter is one piece of the steady stream of notes that passed between the two governments in the spring of 1863.

Confederate warships built in British yards were a sore point all year. Washington pressed London to stop them, and letters like this carried that pressure. The stakes behind this routine mail were high. If Britain had backed the Confederacy, the war could have changed course, so each note helped hold the line of British neutrality. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.
frus-1863p1-d589:
Among the day's business on 17 July 1863 was a letter from Lord Lyons to William H. Seward. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message.

The real subject under all the polite wording was British neutrality. Washington wanted it kept strict, and London wanted no quarrel it could avoid. Much of the mail between the two offices turned on ships: the Union blockade, seized cargoes, and Confederate agents buying vessels in British ports. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1863p1-d689:
The date is 11 November 1863, and the two men are Secretary of State William H. Seward and Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. Their exchange is kept as document 689 in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States.

Routine mail of this kind is the spine of the record for the Civil War years. Grand speeches get the fame, but notes like this one did the steady work. They shared facts, lodged protests, and kept each side aware of the other's view. A reader who follows them in order can track the mood between Washington and London almost day by day through the fall of 1863.
plos-pbio-0020289:
Tammie Bishop, Kah Weng Lau, Andrew C. R. Epstein, and their team used the worm C. elegans to study a tumor suppressor in PLOS Biology in 2004. In humans, loss of the VHL gene causes kidney tumors and blood vessel growth run wild. The worm has its own version of the gene.

By breaking worm genes one by one, the team found which pathways the worm's VHL controls. Worms are far simpler than people, so each link stands out clearly. Several links matched the human picture, which validates the worm as a test system. Others were new leads. The study shows how a tiny animal can sort the wiring of a human cancer gene.
plos-pone-0000089:
Félix Gutierrez, Sergio Padilla, Mar Masiá, and a large team followed HIV patients over the long term in PLOS ONE in 2006. Modern antiretroviral therapy can hold the virus at undetectable levels for years. The team asked how patients who kept that control actually fared in health over time.

Sustained control turned into real gains: fewer AIDS events and better survival than in earlier eras of care. Long follow-up is what proves a therapy's worth beyond lab numbers. Their report captures the moment HIV care shifted from crisis control to chronic disease management. It also sets a standard: new regimens must match this durable success, not just short term viral drops.
plos-pone-0000189:
Aartjan J. W. te Velthuis, Tadamoto Isogai, Lieke Gerrits, and colleagues published this protein evolution paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. The PDZ/LIM family is a set of proteins that organize signaling and the cell skeleton, found across animals. The authors trace the family's molecular evolution and identify a new conserved protein motif within it.

A motif kept across species usually marks a part a protein cannot do without. Finding a new one in a well-studied family opens fresh questions about what these proteins do. The paper gives the family a clearer family tree and a new feature for other researchers to test.
plos-pone-0000289:
Jill M. Ferdinands, David M. Mannino, Marta L. Gwinn, and colleagues published this respiratory study in PLOS ONE in 2007. It draws on the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities study, a large US cohort. The authors examine the ADRB2 gene's Arg16Gly variant, in the beta-2 adrenergic receptor, alongside beta-agonist inhaler use, lung function, and mortality.

Earlier evidence hinted that one genotype might make asthma drugs harmful for some patients. The authors test that worry in a big population sample with long follow-up. Their results help doctors judge whether this common gene variant should change how inhalers are prescribed.
plos-pone-0000389:
Vincent Guiyedi and colleagues studied severe malaria in Gabonese children, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. Cerebral malaria, where the disease attacks the brain, is among its deadliest forms. The team looked at whether the children's immune reactions against alpha spectrin, a protein from their own non-red blood cells, tracked with this severe form.

Self-reactivity means the immune system attacks the body's own proteins, not just the parasite. Finding that such reactions correlate with cerebral malaria suggests the damage is partly self-inflicted by the immune response. That insight could guide efforts to predict which children are at risk of the worst outcomes and to treat the harmful response itself.
plos-pone-0000489:
Rangarajan Sampath and colleagues built a mass spectrometry system to watch flu viruses change worldwide, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Their method performs global surveillance of emerging influenza virus genotypes. It identifies viral strains by the masses of their genetic pieces. That is far faster than slow full sequencing.

Speed is the point: knowing which flu strains are emerging, and where, guides vaccine selection each year. Mass spectrometry can process many samples quickly and flag unusual genotypes for closer study. The paper describes an early high-throughput surveillance platform, built in an era of heightened concern about a possible influenza pandemic.
plos-pone-0000589:
Ilja Mikenberg and colleagues tracked how a master inflammation switch reaches its workplace, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. NF-κB is a transcription factor that turns on immune and stress genes; it must travel from the cell body into the nucleus to work. In hippocampal neurons, the team showed it is transported via the cytoplasmic dynein/dynactin motor complex, the cell's cargo-hauling machinery.

Neurons are long, so how a signal travels from a distant synapse to the nucleus is a real logistics problem. Pinning NF-κB's ride on the dynein motor explains a puzzle. It shows how synaptic events can switch genes on hours later. That step matters in forming lasting memories and in brain inflammation alike.
plos-pone-0000689:
Masatoshi Suzuki, Jacalyn McHugh, Craig Tork and colleagues tested a cell therapy in a rat model of familial ALS for PLOS ONE in 2007. ALS is a fatal, progressive disease where large motor neurons in brain and spinal cord die. Patients lose muscle control and face eventual paralysis. Growth factors such as GDNF can support struggling neurons.

The team used human neural progenitor cells engineered to secrete GDNF. Their title reports a split outcome: the cells protected dying motor neurons, but not the neurons' projections to muscle. Saving the cell body without saving its connection limits the benefit. That distinction tells therapy designers what still needs fixing.
plos-pone-0000789:
Se-Jin Lee reported quadrupling muscle mass in mice by blocking growth-limiting signals, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Myostatin is a member of the TGF-beta family that normally acts to limit skeletal muscle growth. Mice engineered to lack myostatin activity carry about twice the muscle mass throughout the body. Similar effects appear in cattle, sheep, and dogs with natural myostatin mutations.

Doubling was not the ceiling. By targeting TGF-beta signaling pathways more broadly, Lee pushed muscle mass toward four times normal. The pathway matters for muscle-wasting diseases, livestock breeding, and basic questions about how body size is set. Bigger is not automatically healthier, which is why the mechanism matters.
plos-pone-0000889:
Johannes Muller and Linda Tsuji found signs of advanced hearing in early land reptiles, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. A working middle ear that matches sound pressure between air and the inner ear is a mark of sharp hearing in land vertebrates. When that system first appeared was an open question in the story of amniotes, the group that includes reptiles, birds and mammals.

The authors read the fossil evidence for an impedance matching ear in Paleozoic reptiles, from long before mammals existed. Their case pushes refined hearing far back in time. It suggests the first land vertebrates were sensing their world in more detail than often assumed.
plos-pone-0000989:
Catriona Paul, Joanne Povey, Nicola Lawrence and colleagues deleted sperm protecting genes in mice and measured the fallout, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Infertility touches about twenty percent of couples in Europe, and in half the cases the cause lies with the man. Damaged DNA in male germ cells is poorly understood, though it may raise miscarriage risk.

Mouse models let the team remove genes thought to guard germ cell DNA integrity. They then counted DNA breaks and germ cell loss. The deletions did not all act alike; effects differed by gene. That difference itself guides which guards matter most for fertility.
plos-pone-0001089:
Rossarin Suwanarusk and co-authors profiled chloroquine resistance in the other malaria parasite, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Plasmodium vivax causes the second major form of human malaria. Drug treatment failure for vivax had reached high levels in eastern Indonesia, yet its resistance had not been profiled in the lab or tied to gene markers.

Using a modified test of the parasite's blood stage, the team measured resistance directly and checked for links to gene variants. Vivax hides in the liver and relapses, so failing blood treatment compounds the problem. Defined markers would let health officials map resistance without slow culture work.
plos-pone-0001189:
Lymphatic filariasis, a disfiguring disease caused by the parasitic worm Brugia malayi, threatens more than 1.5 billion people. Sanjay Kumar and colleagues mined the worm's genome for drug targets in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The completed draft sequence of the parasite's genome made a genome-wide search possible.

The authors report the first genome-wide application of a rational drug target selection method to a metazoan pathogen. They focused on predicted essential genes, genes the worm likely cannot live without. A shortlist like this gives drug developers concrete starting points against a neglected disease.
plos-pone-0001289:
A high share of male infertility has no known cause. Sahar Houshdaran and colleagues looked for epigenetic defects in the sperm of such men, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Abnormal epigenetic programming of the germline, the chemical marks that organize DNA without changing its code, had been proposed as a mechanism compromising sperm production.

The authors report widespread epigenetic abnormalities in abnormal human sperm, suggesting a broad DNA methylation erasure defect. Erasure is the step that wipes old marks in the germline so new ones can be written. A failure there could underlie many unexplained cases at once.
plos-pone-0001389:
Manjula Pandey, Smita Patel, and Abram Gabriel published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on an enzyme from a yeast element that can copy itself. Enzymes that build DNA use a shared way to add each new unit. The enzyme here works in reverse, building DNA from an RNA guide. The team traced one step of that work in fine detail.

The authors map the path by which the enzyme can also run the build step in reverse. That reverse step can undo gains and shape how the element spreads. Fine maps like this help explain how jumping genes move and change genomes. They also add to the base facts on how all such enzymes work.
plos-pone-0001489:
Irina Tcherepanova and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE methods paper on a tailored HIV therapy. The therapy uses a patient's own immune guide cells loaded with their own virus. Past trials of that plan needed large amounts of live virus, which is hard to get. The team built a way to copy HIV genes in bulk instead.

Their method copies many HIV genes at once from a patient's virus. Those copies can load the guide cells without vast virus stocks. That makes the tailored plan more feasible for clinics. It is a step toward immune care built for each patient's own virus strain.
plos-pone-0001589:
Birger Scholz and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on the Parkinson's drug L-dopa in monkeys. The drug can cause wild, unwanted moves after long use. That harm grows with each dose, a process called sensitization. The team used the standard monkey model to read protein shifts in a key brain zone.

They found the protein pattern after the first dose much like that after long use. In other words, the first dose already sets the long term state. That shifts the search for the harm's roots to the very start of care. It may open a window to block the harm before it builds.
plos-pone-0001689:
Kaspar Delhey and Anne Peters measured how variable bird colors are in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. A key idea in evolution says ornaments used in sexual selection stay highly variable. Bright plumage is one example, and its quality depends on the bearer's condition. Only a bird in good shape can afford a top-grade signal, so condition-dependent models predict signaling traits should vary more than ordinary traits.

The authors quantified color variation across traits and species to test that prediction. The full text gives the color measurements, the comparison between signaling and non-signaling traits, and how strong the difference was. A careful test matters because the prediction is widely assumed in sexual selection theory but had rarely been measured across many birds at once.
plos-pone-0001789:
Tetsuro Tamaki, Akira Akatsuka, Yoshinori Okada, and their co-authors tested muscle-derived stem cells for heart repair in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Cellular cardiomyoplasty, transplanting cells to repair heart attack damage, had been tried with various cell types. None had shown complete differentiation into heart muscle cells, though functional benefits were reported.

The team used skeletal muscle-derived multi-myogenic stem cells, which can form several muscle types, and transplanted them into infarcted myocardium. They report cardiomyocyte formation after transplantation. The full text gives the cell isolation, the transplant model, and the heart tissue results. A patient's own muscle could be an accessible cell source for heart repair if the conversion is real and safe.
plos-pone-0001889:
Luciana Madeira and co-authors hunted a hard-to-spot protein family in malaria parasites in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Serpentine receptors snake through cell walls and pass signals inward; they are found in bacteria, fungi, plants, and animals. Whether the protozoan parasites that cause malaria carry them was largely unknown.

The team searched parasite genomes across the full set of genes for shapes that match this receptor class. Finding such receptors in the parasite would open new drug targets, since these proteins sit on the cell surface where drugs can reach them. The study gives malaria work a fresh parts list to test, gene by gene.
plos-pone-0001989:
Chao Cheng and Lei Li built a way to infer the hidden activity of tiny gene regulators, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The regulators are microRNAs, short RNA pieces that tune how much protein their target genes make. Computer tools existed to find microRNA genes or predict their targets, but not to gauge how active each one is in a sample.

The pair joined two data types: the measured activity of genes, and predictions of which genes each microRNA targets. If a microRNA is active, its targets should dip as a group. That logic turns gene data into a readout of regulators no assay measures directly.
plos-pone-0002089:
Lulla Opatowski and co-authors modeled whether a new drug class could slow resistant pneumococcus spread, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Streptococcus pneumoniae causes pneumonia and other ills, and its resistance to antibiotics keeps rising, yet new antibacterial classes are rare. Ketolides are one of the few new classes active against it in twenty-five years, and they act much like an older class.

The team modeled how ketolide use could affect the dissemination of multiresistant strains. As the title states, antibiotic innovation may contribute to slowing that spread. Models help stewards place a scarce new drug where it does the most good.
plos-pone-0002189:
Evelina Angov, Collette Hillier, Randall Kincaid, and co-authors showed a way to make lab-made proteins come out better, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. When a gene from one organism is placed in another to make its protein, output is often low or the protein clumps into useless lumps. The team suspected that the gene's codon usage, its choice among spellings that mean the same thing, was part of the problem.

By rewriting a target gene so its codon pattern matched that of the host, they raised protein output. The method, called codon harmonization, respects the natural rhythm of protein building instead of simply speeding it up. Better yields matter for making vaccines and research proteins.
plos-pone-0002289:
Pierre-Edouard Fournier, Lokmane Belghazi, Catherine Robert, and co-authors compared the plasmid content of Rickettsia felis strains, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Rickettsia felis is a flea-borne bacterium that causes fever in people. Its characterization was tangled early on because an initial culture was contaminated with a sister species, Rickettsia typhi.

Once a stable culture existed, the species could be described properly, including its plasmids, the small extra rings of DNA bacteria carry. The team found that plasmid content varies between strains. Variation in these mobile elements can affect how labs identify the bacterium and may relate to how it lives in fleas and people.
plos-pone-0002389:
Hoehl and fellow authors published a research article through PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Stefanie Hoehl, Lisa Wiese, Tricia Striano, among others. Its subject is young Infants' Neural Processing of Objects Is Affected by Eye Gaze Direction and Emotional Expression. Eye gaze is an important social cue which is used to determine another person's focus of attention and intention to communicate.

In combination with a fearful facial expression eye gaze can also signal threat in the environment. The piece walks readers through the question, the setup, and the steps that came next. The result is a compact record of the work, of use to readers who study the same problem or teach it to others.
plos-pone-0002489:
Raby and co-authors published a research article in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Edward Raby, Maureen Moyo, Akash Devendra, among others. Its subject is the Effects of HIV on the Sensitivity of a Whole Blood IFN-γ Release Assay. The rest of the title points to Zambian Adults with Active Tuberculosis. Interferon gamma release assays (IGRA) are replacing the tuberculin skin test (TST) as a diagnostic tool for Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection.

However research into the test's performance in the high HIV-TB burden setting is scarce. The paper sets out the problem first and then the line of work the team chose to take. As a record, it keeps the focus on facts and method, and lets readers judge the claims for themselves.
plos-pone-0002589:
Hu, working with fellow researchers, published a study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Jian Hu, Xavier Barlet, Laurent Deslandes, among others. Its subject is transcriptional Responses of Arabidopsis thaliana during Wilt Disease Caused by the Soil-Borne Phytopathogenic Bacterium, Ralstonia solanacearum. Bacterial wilt is a common disease that causes severe yield and quality losses in many plants.

In the present study, we used the model Ralstonia solanacearum - Arabidopsis thaliana pathosystem to study transcriptional changes linked to wilt disease development. The piece walks readers through the question, the setup, and the steps that came next. The full text is free to read, so any reader can check the work and follow the links to past work.
plos-pone-0002689:
In 2008, Hui Liu and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE. Their subject was specific and sensitive detection of H. pylori in biological specimens by Real-Time RT-PCR and in situ hybridization. The catalog record names Hui Liu first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. PCR detection of H. A further point appears in the abstract. Pylori in biological specimens is rendered difficult by the extensive polymorphism of H. The piece stands as a short, open record of the research question and the grounds on which the authors pursued it.
plos-pone-0002789:
In 2008, Nicole Y. K. Li and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE. Their subject was a Patient-Specific in silico model of inflammation and healing tested in acute vocal fold injury. Authorship is credited in the record to Nicole Y. K. Li and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. The development of personalized medicine is a primary objective of the medical community and increasingly also of funding and registration agencies. A further point appears in the abstract. Modeling is generally perceived as a key enabling tool to target this goal. The article gives specialists and general readers a compact entry point into the topic, with its aims and scope stated up front.
plos-pone-0002889:
Alessio Adamo, John W. Pinney, Andrea Kunova and co-authors studied heat stress in the plant Arabidopsis thaliana in 2008. Adding a tail of adenine units to RNA, called polyadenylation, can either protect a transcript or mark it for decay. In plant mitochondria, the power units of the cell, that tail tends to promote decay.

Published in PLOS ONE, the study tracks how heat changes the buildup of tailed mitochondrial transcripts. Heat stress raised that buildup, as the title states. The work adds detail on how plant cells handle RNA damage and turnover when temperatures climb, a growing concern for crops.
plos-pone-0002989:
Thierry Work, Greta Aeby and James Maragos described a reef takeover at Palmyra Atoll in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Coral reefs can shift fast from one dominant life form to another, a change called a phase shift. Human disturbance, pollution, and changes in reef life have all been blamed in past cases.

Here the shift from coral to corallimorph dominance was associated with a shipwreck on the atoll. Corallimorphs are coral-like anemones that can carpet reef surfaces. Documenting a wreck-linked shift gives reef managers a concrete, local cause to act on, unlike diffuse global drivers.
plos-pone-0003089:
Amornrat Anuwatnonthakate, Pranom Limsomboon, Sriprapa Nateniyom and co-authors assessed directly observed therapy for tuberculosis in Thailand in 2008. The World Health Organization recommends that patients receive directly observed therapy, where a watcher confirms each dose. Randomized trials had not consistently shown it improves treatment success.

Thailand is one of 22 high-burden countries named by the WHO. The study evaluates outcomes under observed therapy there at program scale. Published in PLOS ONE, national data help decide whether a labor-intensive policy earns its cost in real practice. The article appeared in PLOS ONE, an open access journal anyone can read free online.
plos-pone-0003189:
Izuho Hatada, Masakazu Namihira, Sumiyo Morita and colleagues study cell fate timing in the developing brain in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Epigenetic changes are thought to alter cell properties such as what a cell can become. Neural precursor cells make only neurons in the mid-stage brain, yet later they become able to generate astrocytes, the star-shaped support cells.

The title reports that astrocyte-specific genes are generally demethylated in precursor cells before astrocyte differentiation begins. Readers learn that preparation for a fate can precede the fate itself. That ordering helps explain how developmental timing is set at the DNA level.
plos-pone-0003289:
Richard G. Carroll, Carmine Carpenito, Xiaochuan Shan and colleagues test a cytokine's effect on human T cells in mice in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. IL-18 has pleiotropic effects on the activation of T cells during antigen presentation. The team investigated effects of human IL-18 on the engraftment and function of human T cell subsets in xenograft mouse models. They report IL-18 enhanced engraftment of human CD8 effector T cells.

The title reports distinct effects of IL-18 on effector CD8 T cells and regulatory T cells. Readers learn that one signal can favour killer cells over calming cells. That balance is central to cancer and transplant immunology.
plos-pone-0007389:
Ryan K. C. Yuen, Luana Avila, Maria S. Peñaherrera, and colleagues studied DNA methylation variation in the placenta in 2009. Variation in methylation levels between individuals is widespread in the human genome. Methylation regulates gene expression, so its variation may shape traits and disease in ways genetics alone cannot explain for human health.

The nature and tissue specificity of that variation were open questions. The authors examine placental-specific epipolymorphism, stable methylation differences in placenta tissue. They test associations with adverse pregnancy outcomes. Their PLOS ONE work links placental epigenetics to complications that affect mothers and babies.
plos-pone-0007489:
Yunping Li and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on how the womb switches from quiet to contracting at labor. The myometrium, the uterus's muscle layer, stays relaxed through pregnancy, then activates. What flips that switch is still incompletely understood. Stretch of the growing uterus has long been suspected as one trigger. The team tested how stretch signals inside human myometrial cells.

Stretch activated the muscle through a chain of signals. ERK, a relay kinase, was involved, along with caldesmon, a protein that tunes contraction. Focal adhesion signaling, the cell's anchor system, also took part. Mapping this chain matters because preterm labor lacks good treatments. Each step in the pathway is a possible point for a drug to calm the uterus. The study connects a physical force to molecular switches.
plos-pone-0007589:
Jin Leng and Eric Denkers published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on how a common parasite edits host gene control. The parasite, Toxoplasma gondii, lives inside macrophages, the very cells meant to kill it. Infected cells fail to make many of the signals that would raise an alarm. One calming signal, IL-10, is left intact. The team looked at the packaging of DNA at the IL-10 gene in infected cells.

The parasite blocks a chemical tag from being set on a histone protein at that gene's start site. The block is precise, sparing IL-10 while other responses are shut down. Such fine control shows a parasite tuning its host, not wrecking the controls. Life inside immune cells takes exactly that touch. The study shows one small edit behind the parasite's long, quiet stay in its hosts.
plos-pone-0007689:
Kay Sin Tan and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It concerns stroke in young patients. Doctors still lack sharp tools to diagnose stroke early and predict how a patient will do. Small RNAs called microRNAs have shown promise as markers in diseases such as cancer and diabetes.

The team profiled microRNAs in young people who had suffered a stroke. A profile is a pattern of which small RNAs are present and at what levels. If such patterns track the disease, they could one day help doctors spot stroke sooner and sort patients by risk.
plos-pone-0007789:
Jun Shen and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It traces how the H1N1 flu virus's surface protein changed since 1918. That protein, hemagglutinin, is the main target of the immune system. The 2009 pandemic strain was then spreading and killing people worldwide.

Symptoms were mostly mild at the time of writing. Fears remained that new mutations could make the virus more dangerous. By mapping evolutionary trends across ninety years, the team sought clues to the virus's future path. Such long views help scientists judge pandemic risk and update vaccines.
plos-pone-0007889:
Guillaume Robert and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It tests a compound that kills a leukemia cell type in an unusual way. Chronic myelogenous leukemia is a blood stem cell disease. It is driven by a fused oncoprotein, BCR-ABL, made by a chromosome swap.

The compound, acadesine, was already known to act against another leukemia. The team found it kills these leukemia cells through autophagic cell death. In that process, cells digest themselves to death. The killing depends on the PKC signaling pathway. A new death route is valuable where standard drugs fail.
plos-pone-0007989:
Lina Han and colleagues read immune signals one blood cell at a time in PLOS ONE in 2009. The signal chain centers on STAT5, a protein that carries growth orders inside blood stem and progenitor cells. In leukemia, that chain goes wrong.

Single-cell reads showed normal and leukemic cells answer the same growth signals in sharply unlike ways. Averages over many cells had blurred those gaps. Seeing the response cell by cell exposes which leukemic cells ignore or twist orders, a detail that may matter for drugs meant to reset the chain.
plos-pone-0008089:
Hiromi Ii and colleagues removed one enzyme in mice and watched fatty livers fare better in PLOS ONE in 2009. The enzyme starts the making of prostaglandins, signal fats tied to inflammation. Mice missing it were fed a rich diet that normally scars the liver with fat and cell damage.

Their livers took far less damage than those of normal mice on the same diet. The enzyme thus helps drive the harm, not merely mark it. Blocking its kin is already common in pain drugs, so the result raises a pointed question about liver-safe uses.
plos-pone-0008189:
Chad A. Glazer and colleagues searched for cancer testis antigens in lung cancer in PLOS ONE in 2009. These antigens are proteins normally made only in germline cells. Many cancers switch them on by mistake. The study focused on non-small cell lung cancer, a common and deadly form. The team wanted antigens that stay silent through epigenetic marks.

They used an integrative screening approach to find genes switched back on together. Genes freed from epigenetic repression could serve as targets for immune therapy. They could also mark tumors for diagnosis. The work maps candidates worth testing in later lung cancer studies.
plos-pone-0008289:
Adlane Ould-yahoui and colleagues studied a protein in brain cells in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. TIMP-1 is known for blocking enzymes that break down tissue scaffolding. It also shows many activities beyond that blocking role. In the central nervous system, TIMP-1 rises strongly in reactive astrocytes and cortical neurons. Its full purpose there was unclear.

The team found a new role for TIMP-1 in neurite outgrowth. Neurites are the branches neurons grow to connect with others. TIMP-1 also shaped the morphology of cortical neurons. That role may matter for brain repair after injury.
plos-pone-0008389:
Beena E. Thomas and colleagues studied tuberculosis patients in south India in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Offering HIV testing to tuberculosis patients is a policy called provider-initiated testing and counseling. Its acceptability in Asian settings with concentrated HIV epidemics was not known. A pilot of the policy ran in public health systems in two Indian districts. The team asked patients for their perceptions.

Understanding patient views decides whether such testing can work at scale. Tuberculosis and HIV often travel together, so linked testing saves lives. The study reports what patients thought of being offered the test. It informs combined care programs.
plos-pone-0008489:
Nobuko Yamanaka and co-authors report a transplant finding in mice in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Mouse models help test what human stem cells can do. Bone marrow transplants are the classic test for blood stem cells. But reading results for other organs can be tricky. Cells may pick up marks from the host that confuse the picture. The team transplant human marrow into mice.

They find human donor blood cells gain mouse antigens on their surface. Those antigens include mouse MHC class I and CD45. The cells display host marks without being mouse cells. This warns researchers to judge transplant data with care.
plos-pone-0008589:
Richard Festa and co-authors catalog a protein tagging system in tuberculosis in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Mycobacterium tuberculosis has a small protein modifier called Pup. Pup is the first known such modifier in prokaryotes, or bacteria. It targets proteins for degradation by a bacterial proteasome. That process is akin to ubiquitin-mediated protein destruction in human cells. The team map the Pup proteome, all proteins tagged by Pup in this germ.

Their catalog lists substrates marked for destruction in Mtb. Knowing them reveals how the germ recycles proteins to survive. The Pup system is absent in humans, making it an attractive drug target. Blocking it could weaken TB without harming human cells.
plos-pone-0008689:
Doreen Becker, Jens Tetens, Adrian Brunner, and colleagues investigated blind lambs in Texel sheep. Their 2010 PLOS ONE report centers on a birth defect called microphthalmia. Affected lambs are born with tiny eyes or no eyes at all. They cannot see. The flaw runs in families in a recessive pattern.

Using a chip that reads many DNA markers at once, the team tracked the faulty spot. The trail led to PITX3, a gene that guides early body building. One small change in that gene tracked with the defect. Breeders can now test sheep and avoid pairings that produce blind lambs.
plos-pone-0008789:
Bérénice Benayoun, Sandrine Caburet, Aurélie Dipietromaria, and colleagues probed a mutation found in nearly all tumors of one ovarian kind. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Adult granulosa cell tumors carry a single change in the FOXL2 gene. The change swaps one protein building block for another. Its presence in most cases marks it as a likely driver. A driver mutation must change cell behavior, though.

Lab tests explored what the altered FOXL2 protein does differently. Changes in gene switching and cell survival emerged. Understanding the driver's tricks may expose weak points in these tumors. Such insight guides targeted treatment design.
plos-pone-0008889:
Stanislaw Kaczmarczyk, Kalavathy Sitaraman, Thomas Hill, and colleagues found mammal-style address labels inside a bacterial protein. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Tus is an E. coli protein that stops DNA copying forks. Mammalian cells move proteins between nucleus and cytoplasm using signal tags. Import tags and export tags act like zip codes. A bacterial protein had no obvious need for such labels.

Yet Tus carried separate signals that work in mammalian cells. The signals sent it into the nucleus and back out again. Cross-kingdom labels hint at deep, shared protein-sorting logic. Engineers could borrow Tus signals for moving proteins in gene therapy.
plos-pone-0008989:
Maria Thaller and co-authors checked gut bacteria of Galápagos land iguanas for drug resistance, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Antibiotic resistance spreads fast among bacteria near people and livestock. Antibiotic use in medicine and farming drives that spread. Remote iguanas, living apart from humans, offered a natural control group.

The team screened harmless gut bacteria from the iguanas for acquired resistance. True to the paper's subtitle, no people nearby meant no resistance found. The result supports the idea that human antibiotic use seeds resistance in wildlife. Islands like the Galápagos give science a rare before-picture of a global problem.
plos-pone-0009089:
Giang Vu and co-authors merged two genome-mapping jobs into one protocol, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Sequencing a genome needs a skeleton map to assemble against. Physical maps and linkage maps were traditionally built separately, then merged. The parts used here are BACs, large cloned chunks of DNA.

Their method, BAC-HAPPY mapping, ties physical pieces to linkage positions directly. It grows out of the HAPPY mapping technique for breaking DNA into panels. One workflow replaces two, saving time in genome projects. Cleaner skeleton maps make the finished genome sequence more trustworthy.
plos-pone-0009189:
Tim Hohm, Eckart Zitzler, and Rüdiger Simon published this plant modeling study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Plants keep small pools of stem cells at their growing tips, called meristems. Those pools supply fresh cells for new leaves and stems throughout the plant's life. The puzzle is how the pool stays the right size while the tip keeps growing.

The authors built a dynamic computer model of the meristem in Arabidopsis, a small flowering plant used widely in labs. Their model tracks the signals that tell cells to stay as stem cells or to start specializing. It shows how feedback between cells can hold the stem cell zone steady. Plant scientists can use it to predict how gene changes alter growth patterns.
plos-pone-0009289:
Etsuko Miyamoto-Sato and co-authors published this genomics resource paper in PLOS ONE in 2010. Maps of protein interactions help researchers understand how cells are wired. Existing maps say which proteins touch, but not where they touch. Without contact regions, the maps stay blurry.

The authors built a resource focused on the interacting regions of proteins. They aimed it at transcription factors, the proteins that switch genes on and off. Knowing the exact contact patches refines the network maps of gene control. Other researchers can use the resource to predict new links and to design experiments that test them.
plos-pone-0011389:
Daniel Melamed and co-authors reported in 2010 on how yeast cells keep their walls strong at the spot where a new cell buds off. Budding stretches the wall at a tender point, and a known repair pathway guards that spot. The team studied a protein called Asc1 and its role near bud sites during growth.

They found that Asc1 supports wall strength at bud sites through a route that does not need the well-known repair signal Pkc1. That independence means yeast keeps at least two separate systems guarding the same weak point. Redundancy of this kind is a clue to how single-celled fungi survive stress and antifungal drugs. For researchers, splitting wall care into parallel systems refines the map of how yeast holds its shape while it grows.
plos-pone-0011489:
Michelle Re and co-authors reported in 2010 that a famous hormone receptor works in an unexpected place: inside the cell, on the membrane around the nucleus. The GnRH receptor catches the hormone that governs reproduction, and textbooks place such receptors on the cell surface. The team tested whether the human type I receptor also sits on the nuclear membrane and works there as a functional receptor.

Their evidence says it does, signaling from the nuclear membrane rather than only receiving orders at the surface. Moving a textbook receptor indoors rewrites how reproductive hormone signals are thought to reach the genome. A receptor beside the DNA could tune gene activity with unusual directness. The finding invites a second look at other receptors assumed to work only at the surface, and may change how fertility drugs are designed.
plos-pone-0011589:
Peter Stachon and colleagues tested a suspected driver of clogged arteries in PLOS ONE in 2010. The suspect was TRAF6, a signalling protein that relays messages from several inflammation triggers. Lab work had hinted that TRAF6 promotes inflammation, making it a plausible culprit in plaque build-up inside artery walls.

The team found the opposite of what many expected. Mice lacking TRAF6 still developed artery plaque, and human data showed no link between TRAF6 and the disease either. A clear negative result like this is valuable, because it steers drug research away from a target unlikely to help patients.
plos-pone-0011689:
Nagadenahalli Siddappa and co-authors built laboratory virus strains for AIDS vaccine research, in PLOS ONE in 2010. HIV clade C dominates infections worldwide, so vaccines against it are urgently needed. Antibodies that neutralise the virus are thought to be important, but coaxing the body to make them has proved very difficult.

The team characterised monkey viruses carrying clade C envelopes, classed by how easily antibodies neutralise them. These tiered strains give researchers standard tools to study how the envelope evolves and to test vaccine candidates in primates. Better tools should sharpen the long search for an effective AIDS vaccine.
plos-pone-0011789:
Hongjie Wang and co-authors linked gene-driven variation in an immune protein to diabetes risk, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune disease arising from genes, environment and the immune system together. Genome-wide studies had suggested more than forty susceptibility regions, but how most of them act remained unknown.

The team showed expression of the gene ERBB3, set by a person's DNA, modulates how antigen-presenting cells function. Those cells show targets to the immune attackers that destroy insulin-producing cells. A DNA-set dial on presentation reveals one tunable step on the road to autoimmunity.
plos-pone-0011889:
Glenn Manthey and Adam Bailis studied in 2010 how yeast keeps DNA repair from going wrong. Radiation and other damage can snap both strands of DNA, and cells fix the breaks by copying from matching sequences. With so many repeated sequences in a genome, a repair can mistakenly join two different chromosomes, forming a translocation.

Their work shows the protein Rad51 preventing such translocations when repair takes a non-conservative path. Rad51 is best known for helping recombination happen, so a guarding role adds balance to its reputation. Understanding how cells keep repairs faithful matters for cancer, since translocations are among the changes that can start it.
plos-pone-0011989:
Tim Lynch and co-workers reviewed in 2010 how doctors diagnose bacterial pneumonia in children, and how shaky the reference standards are. Pneumonia is a leading killer of children under five in developing countries, and it is a common cause of illness in North America too. Clinicians traditionally lean on certain tests as if they were gold standards.

The systematic review argues that the supposed gold standard is really bronze: the reference tests themselves misclassify cases. When the yardstick is bent, every accuracy claim measured against it bends too. The review urges better reference methods before new rapid tests for childhood pneumonia are judged.
plos-pone-0012089:
Matthew Dyer, Chris Neff, Max Dufford, and colleagues mapped how three dangerous bacteria interact with human proteins, in a PLOS ONE paper from 2010. The germs cause anthrax, tularemia, and plague, and all three rank among the most feared possible bioweapon threats. The team built networks showing which human proteins each germ touches once it reaches human cells.

A shared map lets readers compare the three germs side by side instead of studying each one alone. Points where the networks overlap may show common weak spots in how these infections take hold. Such maps guide later work on drugs and defenses that could work against more than one threat at once.
plos-pone-0012189:
Joseph Milanovich, William Peterman, Nathan Nibbelink, and co-authors forecast the fate of Appalachian salamanders under climate change, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The southern Appalachians hold the world's richest variety of lungless salamanders, animals that breathe through their skin and cannot travel far. Creatures that need cool, wet homes and move slowly are exactly those a warming climate squeezes hardest.

Their models project a sharp loss of suitable habitat for these salamanders as conditions warm. The forecast gives conservationists a map of where refuges may survive and where losses will strike first. Protecting those pockets early is far cheaper than mourning a hotspot that science saw coming.
plos-pone-0012289:
Xin Gao, Zhengyuan Wang, John Martin, and co-authors mapped gene targets of a survival switch in hookworm, in PLOS ONE in 2010. A young hookworm waits in the soil in suspended animation, unable to feed or grow until it finds a host to infect. The dog hookworm stands in for the human parasites in research, and a stress-and-longevity switch called DAF-16 is suspected of running that waiting state.

The team found the DNA response elements the switch binds and listed the genes it directly controls. Those targets are the machinery of suspended life, and some may be unique enough to attack with drugs. Hookworm infects hundreds of millions of people, so its waiting-state secrets have real weight.
plos-pone-0012389:
Bruno Pairet and Elmar Jaenicke solved the shape of guinea pig hemoglobin in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Guinea pigs live well at high altitude, and their blood grabs oxygen more tightly than that of lowland animals. The authors froze the protein in one of its working shapes, the R2 state, and read its structure at fine detail.

The structure shows small changes in the protein that favor tight oxygen binding. Those tweaks explain how the animal thrives in thin mountain air. Comparing this shape with human hemoglobin deepens the basic science of oxygen transport and informs work on blood substitutes and diseases where oxygen delivery fails.
plos-pone-0012489:
Heidi Vebø, Margrete Solheim, Lars Snipen and colleagues compared harmful and helpful strains of Enterococcus faecalis, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. This bacterium is the top enterococcal cause of urinary tract infections, yet some strains are sold as probiotics. Telling dangerous strains from safe ones by genome could prevent harm and guide probiotic screening.

The team compared genomes of disease and probiotic isolates and read their gene activity while growing in human urine. The comparisons reveal traits that track with infection ability. Such trait lists give regulators and doctors a sharper basis for judging which live bacteria are safe to give patients.
plos-pone-0012589:
Michaël Boele van Hensbroek, Job Calis, Kamija Phiri and colleagues investigated severe anaemia in Malawian children, in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. Severe anaemia is a major killer of African children, yet its causes are many, and programs often targeted only one or two — malaria or worms — with disappointing results. A full accounting of causes in one setting was needed.

The study weighed the many contributing factors together, from infections and nutrition to inherited blood traits. Their combined picture shows single-cause campaigns cannot fix a multi-cause problem. Malawi's experience guides integrated child health programs across the region, where transfusions and single supplements have repeatedly fallen short.
plos-pone-0012689:
Solmesky, Lefler, Jacob-Hirsch and co-authors set up a clean test bed using human bone marrow stem cells. These mesenchymal stem cells stick to plastic dishes, renew themselves and can form several tissue types. Their 2010 study grew them without serum, the animal fluid that usually feeds lab cells.

Serum-free growth removes a noisy ingredient, so the effects of single added molecules stand out clearly. That clean setup lets researchers screen drugs and signals on human stem cells with fewer false leads. It also suits future medical use, where animal products raise safety worries.
plos-pone-0012789:
Eduati, Corradin, Di Camillo and co-authors entered a contest to predict cell signalling, using a yes-no logic model. The DREAM4 challenge asked teams to forecast how protein signals would behave, from limited test data. Their 2010 entry used Boolean logic, treating each signal as simply on or off.

Even that coarse view can capture a network's main behaviour surprisingly well. Simple models are fast to run and easy to read, advantages when data are scarce. Their result helps set fair expectations for what prediction methods can do.  The challenge data came from single perturbation experiments.
pmc-1563489:
Raj, Peskin, Tranchina, and co-authors study why identical cells make uneven amounts of messenger RNA. Even in a uniform group, single cells have been found to hold different counts of a given protein. The team asked where that variation begins in mammalian cells.

They counted single mRNA molecules made from a test gene, one cell at a time. Their counts show that production comes in bursts rather than a steady flow, which explains much of the spread. Burst-like production is now a basic idea in how scientists think about noise and chance inside cells.
pmc-4086089:
Biasini, Bienert, Waterhouse, and their colleagues described SWISS-MODEL in 2014. The server builds three-dimensional models of proteins from their sequences. Such homology modelling, which copies the shape of a known related protein, had become routine when no measured structure exists.

SWISS-MODEL is fully automated and works through a friendly web interface. Users get a reliable model without needing complex local software or deep expertise. The method uses evolutionary information, since related proteins tend to keep the same fold. These models help researchers plan experiments, explain mutations, and search for drug binding sites on new proteins.
pmc-4246889:
Wang, Liang, and Zen reviewed in 2014 the molecular mechanisms that set the balance between macrophage types. Macrophages are a core part of innate immunity and can either slow or drive cell growth and tissue repair. Variety and flexibility are their hallmarks, the authors stress.

The review contrasts classical M1 activation, which fights germs and inflames, with alternative M2 activation, which heals. It maps the signals and gene switches that push cells toward either pole. That balance goes wrong in infection, cancer, and chronic wounds. Knowing the controls points to ways drugs might nudge macrophages toward the state a patient needs.
pmc-5073889:
Becht, Giraldo, Lacroix, and their co-authors introduced MCP-counter in 2016. The method estimates how many tissue-infiltrating immune and stromal cells are present in a tissue sample, using gene expression data. Tissues are heterogeneous, mixing many cell types, which hides who is actually there.

MCP-counter gives a robust count of how abundant each of eight immune cell types and two stromal types is. The authors validated it with in vitro mixtures of messenger RNA of known makeup. Knowing a tumor's immune makeup helps predict its course and its response to immunotherapy. A method that works on standard expression data makes such estimates widely available.
pmc-6891889:
Maigeng Zhou, Haidong Wang, Xinying Zeng, and coauthors analyzed health in China and its provinces in 2019. China holds about a fifth of the world's people, and its government treats public health as a priority. Province-level evidence is what policy actually needs.

Using Global Burden of Disease data, the study tracks deaths, disease, and risk factors province by province. Stroke and heart disease lead, while smoking and diet risks loom large. Richer coastal provinces look very different from inland ones. The results guide where China should aim its prevention spending first.
pmc-7245089:
Xu and co-authors reported in 2020 on treating patients with severe COVID-19 using tocilizumab, a drug that blocks the receptor for interleukin-6. Their reasoning starts from the biology of severe disease, where large numbers of immune cells switch on and release signaling proteins. That flood of signals can drive a dangerous whole body inflammatory reaction often called a cytokine storm.

The authors describe giving the drug to severely ill patients and watching how their condition changed afterward. Their report argued that blocking this one immune signal could calm the harmful response. Coming early in the pandemic, when few proven treatments existed, the work drew wide attention to immune calming drugs as a path worth testing in larger, stricter trials.
pmc-7385689:
Valentina Puntmann and colleagues asked in 2020 what COVID-19 leaves behind in the heart after patients seem to have recovered. They studied one hundred patients recently recovered from the infection, found through a testing center rather than through heart complaints. Each person received detailed heart imaging with cardiac magnetic resonance, a scan that can reveal swelling, scarring, and weakened pumping.

The scans showed signs of heart involvement in a striking share of these recovered patients, including in some who had not been severely ill. That finding shifted attention from the lungs alone to the need for follow up care after infection. It also raised open questions, still debated, about how lasting such heart changes are and what they mean for long term health.
plos-pone-0351589:
Lingyao Sun and six colleagues published this study protocol in PLOS ONE in 2026. A protocol sets out a research plan before the work is done. Here the planned work is a systematic review, combined with a network meta-analysis, of treatments for adults with simple obesity.

The document explains how the team will search for trials, judge their quality, and compare many treatments against each other, including ones never tested head to head. Publishing the plan in advance keeps the later review honest and open to checking. Clinicians who treat obesity will be the main readers of the finished review this protocol describes.
plos-pone-0357089:
Sanchit Vashisht, Shalli Rani, and Fazlullah Khan wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on road safety. It presents TRIDENT-Risk, an AI-driven framework for forecasting high-severity accident risk before crashes happen. The system is a temporal ensemble, combining several models whose inputs unfold over time, built for intelligent transportation systems.

Forecasting severe crashes, rather than all accidents, targets the events that kill and maim. City traffic centers could use advance risk warnings to adjust signals, patrols, or speed limits at dangerous hours. Transport authorities and smart-city engineers are the audience for a proactive system of this kind.
plos-pone-0360189:
Innocent Ayesiga, David Tenywa, and Moses Ntaro wrote this protocol in PLOS ONE in 2026. It plans a scoping review of how facilities across sub-Saharan Africa's health services run their systems for reporting workplace hazards and incidents. A scoping review maps what systems exist and what is known about them.

Health workers face needle injuries, infections, and violence at work, yet incidents often go unreported where systems are weak. Mapping reporting systems first shows where evidence and practice stand before deeper reviews follow. Hospital safety officers and African health ministries are the audience for this groundwork on protecting staff.
plos-pone-0349489:
Kuenyoul Park, Joonsang Yu, Wonho Choe, and Soo Jin Yoo published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It evaluates blood collection tubes from a system called UNI-VAC, covering serum separator, EDTA, sodium citrate, and sodium fluoride types. The comparison benchmark is the widely used Vacutainer tubes from Becton, Dickinson and Company.

Tube choice can quietly shift laboratory results, since each additive preserves blood differently. A head-to-head evaluation tells hospital laboratories whether a newer supplier's tubes match the standard they trust. Laboratory managers weighing purchasing decisions, and clinicians who depend on comparable results, are the readers for this practical test.
plos-pone-0358689: Buffardi and two co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE review on housing as a route to better health. As a scoping review, it maps policy actions that aim to improve health by changing homes or housing access. The map shows what kinds of programs exist and where evidence is thin. Housing shapes health through damp, cold, crowding, and cost, so a clear map helps funders choose wisely.
plos-pone-0358989: Aji and six co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on tiny zinc oxide particles made in a greener way. The particles are meant to help waxy crude oil keep flowing. Wax can thicken oil and clog pipes as it cools. The team made the particles and described their traits in detail. Flow helpers made sustainably could cut the cost and waste of keeping oil moving.
plos-pone-0359089: Tian and five co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on forecasting the course of acute pancreatitis. Pancreatitis is a sudden, painful swelling of the pancreas that can turn deadly. The team tested two blood-based scores: one built from glucose and fat levels, the other a ratio tied to inflammation and nutrition. They asked how well each predicts severity and death within twenty-eight days.
plos-pone-0353989: Li and one co-author published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on how stock markets react to drug policy news in China. Reactions were not uniform: they varied across drug industry subsectors and across time scales. A policy that lifts one branch, like vaccine makers, may dent another. Investors and policy makers alike benefit from knowing which parts of the sector move, and for how long.

gao-gaoreports-b-310489: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by Superlative Technologies, Inc. Decided January 4, 2008, it reviews whether the agency ran a fair competition. europmc-pmc8346589: Published in 2021, this research paper takes on an omics-based framework for assessing the health risk of antimicrobial resistance (germs beating drugs) genes. the-constitution-of-the-empire-of-japan-: The Meiji Constitution, the document that turned Japan into a modern constitutional state in 1889.
