moby-dick-or-the-whale-pg2489: This edition of Melville's Moby Dick: Ahab's hunt for the white whale, in all its terrible glory. The great American novel, vast as the sea it describes. Ishmael's voyage into the heart of obsession. Melville's whale is the most famous in literature.
memoirs-of-the-court-of-marie-antoinette: This volume of the queen's memoirs turns toward public trouble and disgrace. The court's careless extravagance feeds the growing anger of the people. plos-pone-0358589:
Reinhard Fuchs leads a team of eight testing a hands free way to measure blood flow during resuscitation, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Chest compressions vary in quality, yet rescuers have no easy meter for the blood those compressions actually move. The group mounted an ultrasound Doppler probe on a standard neck collar, using an inflatable cushion to hold steady pressure, aiming for semiautomatic readings without a free hand.

One hundred two healthy volunteers wore the device for about half an hour on average. Pain ratings were very low, support ratings near the top of the scale, and no skin irritation appeared. Clear Doppler sounds were captured in over ninety percent of volunteers, and usable flow curves in about three quarters. The study is an early usability step toward feedback that could tell rescuers whether their compressions are working.
plos-pone-0358789:
Sophie Merrick leads a team of eight listening to kidney cancer patients who took immune therapy after surgery, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The interviews sit inside RAMPART, a large international trial testing whether checkpoint inhibitors after kidney removal can stop the cancer returning. Standard quality of life questionnaires predate this drug class. So the team interviewed twenty-three UK participants, chosen to span good and bad treatment experiences. They wanted to learn what the therapy actually does to a life.

Two themes organized their accounts. The first was living in a changed body and mind, as immune side effects altered energy, gut, and mood. The second was context: the same side effect landed differently depending on a person's work, family, and stage of life. How long effects lasted weighed heavily with participants. The study argues that trial measurement must catch duration and life context, not just symptom checklists.
plos-pone-0357989:
Yuan Ding led a team of five authors studying a plant compound and joint cartilage, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. The compound, isoquercitrin, comes from plants and belongs to a group known for protective effects in cells. The team studied worn cartilage cells, the kind that fail in osteoarthritis.

Ding's group found that the compound eased cell dysfunction by acting on a protein called AKT1 and on how the cells manage their mitochondria, their energy centers. Healthier cartilage cells in the lab mark the compound as a candidate worth further testing. Osteoarthritis has few drugs that slow it, so even early cell-level leads draw interest from researchers hunting for gentler options.
plos-pone-0356689:
Roberta Z J McGuinness, Nichole Fairbrother, and Fiona L Challacombe published a review protocol on anxiety around childbirth, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Perinatal anxiety affects many mothers, and it does not always fade after delivery; for some it lasts for years. Their protocol sets out a systematic review and combined analysis of its long-term course.

McGuinness and her colleagues published the plan in advance, defining what studies count and how results will be merged. That advance plan keeps the later synthesis rigorous and open to checking. Clinicians who screen new mothers need to know how long anxiety can persist to plan follow-up. A sound synthesis will show whether services should extend support well beyond the first months.
plos-pone-0354989:
Marina Treskova led a team of eight authors setting out a trial protocol in rural Thailand, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Diseases that jump from animals to people, called zoonotic diseases, pose a daily risk where families live close to livestock. The Saan Suk trial will test an education program tailored to each community, built on One Health ideas.

Treskova's protocol describes a cluster randomized trial in Chanthaburi province, comparing villages that receive the tailored teaching with those that do not. Outcomes cover both knowledge and daily practices. Local tailoring is the bet: generic leaflets rarely change habits. If the trial shows real change, its design can guide zoonotic prevention across rural Southeast Asia.
plos-pone-0357789:
Abdulah J Alqahtani led a team of eight authors tracking drug-resistant staph in Saudi Arabia, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Staphylococcus aureus that resists methicillin is a standing threat in hospitals. The team reviewed lab isolates from the Aseer region across the years 2013 to 2024, a span of more than a decade.

Alqahtani's retrospective study charts how resistance and non-susceptibility to other drugs moved over time. Clinicians choosing antibiotics need exactly this local trend data, since national averages can mislead. Rising resistance argues for tighter prescribing and infection control; stable trends show where current policy works. A long record from one region gives Saudi health officials a firm base for their next steps.
plos-pone-0357889:
Thomas E Diaz and three colleagues hunted for radiation protection among existing drugs, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Astronauts face cosmic radiation that raises cancer and other risks, and developing new drugs takes decades. The team used bioinformatics to reposition approved drugs, screening them for protective potential against space radiation.

Diaz's computational screen searches among medicines whose safety is already known. A hit could move toward testing far faster than a new compound. Space agencies need such options as missions aim for the Moon and Mars, where radiation exposure grows. Repositioning also suits rare Earth uses, such as protecting staff in nuclear incidents. The study lays out candidates and a method others can extend.
plos-pone-0356389:
Marie Anne El Khoury led a team of six authors validating a psychology scale in Arabic, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Fear of happiness is the belief that joy invites disaster, a real pattern that is under-studied in Arabic-speaking populations. The team tested the scale's Arabic version with a sample of adults in Lebanon.

El Khoury's psychometric work checks whether the translated scale measures the trait steadily and truly. A validated tool lets researchers study how this fear relates to depression and daily choices in Lebanon and beyond. Translation alone is not enough; beliefs about emotion differ across cultures, so local testing matters. The study gives Arabic-language mental health research a firmer instrument.
plos-pone-0357289:
Chenxiao Yue led a team of six authors comparing two ways of looking at the world, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. We scan scenes freely when browsing, but hunt in a focused way when searching for something. The team used eye tracking to compare free viewing with goal-directed search and their effects on visual attention.

Yue's gaze patterns reveal precisely how purpose reshapes seeing: where eyes land first, how long they linger, and what they skip. Designers of displays, advertisements, and safety signs all depend on such knowledge. Search behavior also matters for training, from radiology to baggage screening, where missing a target has costs. The study offers clean basic evidence on a skill humans use every waking hour.
plos-pone-0357589:
Frederick Grinnell, Simon Dalley, and Joan Reisch published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE on what high school science fair students actually do to communicate their research. National science standards treat communicating information as a core practice, yet nobody had mapped how fair participants use it. They surveyed students nationally across two school years, asking which of seven communication activities, from keeping a notebook to facing judges, their projects involved.

Nearly eighteen hundred answered. Poster preparation was the most common activity, used by about two-thirds, while only about one in six had done a literature review. Students reported three skills on average. Poster boards and judge interviews were picked far more often than notebooks and literature reviews, the quieter work behind a project. Students using more communication skills reported better fair outcomes, the research notebook standing out. The pattern suggests fairs reward showmanship over documentation, a gap teachers could close.
plos-pone-0347189:
Komal Komal and coauthors published a 2026 engineering study in PLOS ONE on a smart headband that reads brain waves through embroidered electrodes. Standard EEG caps are bulky, slow to fit, need wet gels that irritate skin, and cost too much for everyday monitoring outside labs. The team's neoprene headband carries six soft textile electrodes over the front and sides of the head, tested on ten healthy volunteers against a commercial sponge-electrode system.

The headband caught the classic signatures reliably: the alpha rhythm change between eyes open and closed. It also caught the brain's response blips to rare sounds and rare sights in oddball tasks, all at significance levels matching the commercial gear. Questionnaires gave the headband a clear comfort edge, with no skin irritation reported. Comfortable, modular textile electrodes, they argue, can move brain monitoring into homes and clinics for long sessions, provided larger validation follows.
plos-pone-0343189:
Tasnim Alam and Shangida Akther use computer tools alone to hunt for risky gene changes tied to tuberous sclerosis, a growth disorder that forms benign tumors in many organs. Their 2026 paper studies two human genes whose protein pair normally brakes a key growth signal inside cells. They screen small single-letter changes that swap one building block of the proteins for another.

A dozen checking tools, plus stability and shape models, flagged a small set of changes as most likely harmful in each gene. The flagged spots sit in regions that stayed similar across species and may disturb chemical tags the proteins need. Alam and Akther offer the list as a guide for lab teams deciding which changes deserve costly hands-on testing first.
plos-pone-0345189:
Maria Cisneros and fellow researchers test whether a quiet nose bacterium marks healthier airways in children. The bacterium lives in the back of the nose and has been suspected of guarding against worse germs. Samples came from about one hundred forty children in three groups: healthy, mild viral illness, and severe pneumococcal disease, the dangerous end of chest infection.

The bacterium appeared in well over half of the children, but unevenly: most often in healthy children, less in mild illness, and least in severe disease. Boys carried it more often than girls. Cisneros and colleagues say the pattern supports a protective role worth testing directly, and hints that nose ecology could one day guide prevention of serious chest infections.
plos-pone-0355189:
Laura Henry, Julie S Wilson, Jason J Wilson, and Esther R Beck map what exercise programs for breast cancer survivors actually contain, focusing on the arm swelling that can follow treatment. Activity is advised in survivorship care, yet fear of worsening the swelling keeps many women inactive, and program details vary wildly. The review gathered dozens of primary studies across five databases plus grey sources.

Most programs were controlled trials built around resistance training, commonly running about three months under supervision. Participants had usually had armpit node surgery, radiation, or both. Henry and colleagues chart how swelling was measured and where programs were delivered, exposing gaps in reporting and variety. Their map gives designers a base for building programs survivors can trust.
plos-pone-0348689:
Juan P Zuluaga, Katherine Bedoya-Urrego, and Juan F Alzate build a DNA-based surveillance method for parasitic roundworms hiding in water, sludge, and food. Classic worm hunting relies on microscopes and scarce expertise. Their framework reads a ribosomal gene region from environmental samples. The samples came from Colombia's Andean region. They included treatment plant water and sludge, farm bio-inputs, and foods. The sequences were placed on family trees to name the worms.

Two dozen worm sequence types from six taxa appeared. Several are serious human parasites, including whipworm, pinworm, and hookworm, and two animal-linked species with human risk also showed up. Zuluaga and colleagues argue the method can scale routine environmental watch for parasites in regions where lab capacity is thin.
plos-pone-0354089:
Katrin Kochems and a Dutch team merged two separate palliative care tools into one shared working method. They then tested how to get twenty care teams actually using it. Their study ran from 2020 to 2022 and appeared in 2026. It covered primary care practices, hospices, and nursing homes. Nurses, doctors, and other professionals adjusted the method through three rounds of trial and feedback.

Teams found the shared method workable and welcome. They said it helped them spot palliative needs earlier. It kept care centered on the person, and it gave nurses a stronger voice in planning. Fourteen content changes came out of the trials. The study shows how merging rival tools, with the users in the room, can improve end-of-life care teamwork.
plos-pone-0356989:
Charlotte Verbeke and seven colleagues surveyed people living with multiple myeloma, a blood cancer, and the professionals who treat them, across several countries in late 2023. Their 2026 study asked how much patients know about shared decision-making, how involved they currently feel in treatment choices, and how involved they want to be.

Nearly every patient wanted a say in treatment decisions, and patients reported feeling more involved at recent appointments than at diagnosis. Yet over half of patients, and more than a quarter of professionals, had never heard of shared decision-making as a concept. No personal trait predicted who wanted involvement. The gap is practical, the authors argue: willingness is there on both sides, but clinics need routines that turn willingness into real conversations.
plos-pone-0356889:
Fei Meng and colleagues present ASWBoost, a strengthened version of the classic AdaBoost classification algorithm, aimed at messy real-world data where examples are noisy and one class vastly outnumbers the other. Their 2026 paper modifies the penalty function that decides how hard the algorithm pushes on hard examples, adding a tunable parameter that softens the pull of likely mislabeled outliers.

New update rules follow from that change, and the authors prove bounds on training error and analyze how the parameter shapes convergence. Across synthetic and public datasets, ASWBoost beat AdaBoost and several other boosting variants on balanced accuracy and related measures, matching a leading commercial-grade method overall. Fraud detection and medical screening are typical tasks where such stubborn, lopsided data is the norm.
plos-pone-0355689:
Nuri Peker and colleagues examined what becomes of IVF embryos that fertilize in an odd way. These embryos show one or three pronuclei instead of the normal two. The patients had no normal embryos to use. Their 2026 study tracked fifteen hundred eggs' worth of outcomes at a fertility center. It compared blastocyst formation, genetic test results, and pregnancy across the normal and abnormal groups.

Abnormal embryos reached the blastocyst stage less often for the one-pronucleus group. Every genetically tested abnormal blastocyst came back chromosomally abnormal. So none was transferred on test results. A handful of untested transfers followed, yielding a single pregnancy from a combined transfer. The data counsel great caution. Abnormal fertilization rarely means a usable embryo, and genetic screening is decisive.
plos-pone-0356789:
Issued by the PLOS One staff in 2026, this short notice corrects an earlier study of hepatitis B reactivation during lymphoma treatment. The patients in that study had both surface antigen and viral DNA tests negative. It fixes a results table, removes a duplicated percent sign from treatment-duration data, and replaces several sentences in the abstract and results with their correct wording.

The corrected text states that reactivation rates did not differ significantly by patient gender or by how long treatment lasted. Readers who cite the original study should use these corrected figures. The underlying clinical question matters for doctors deciding how closely to monitor lymphoma patients for a hepatitis B flare during therapy.
plos-pone-0353389:
Paige Copeland and colleagues charted, hour by hour, how eating cannabis affects thinking and movement. Edible cannabis is common, yet the timing of its effects was poorly mapped. Their 2026 study gave fifteen infrequent users a standard dose and ran a test battery eleven times across six hours, with some repeating the session drug-free.

Users felt drug effects from the first hour through the sixth. Reaction time slowed across that same span. Accuracy on a response-control task dropped from about ninety minutes onward, and short-term memory performance dipped for several hours. Heart rate and blood pressure rose in the middle window. Copeland and colleagues identify three to four hours after eating as the peak testing window.
plos-pone-0355989:
Charleen Silcock and co-authors heard Pacific people with Parkinson's in Aotearoa New Zealand, plus their kin. Few brain ills are spreading faster than Parkinson's. Yet Pacific voices on it were near absent. Their 2026 study used talanoa, a Pacific way of learning through shared talk, with Pacific staff in the lead.

One big picture held the talks: life with the illness as a trip the whole kin group takes as one. Folks told of first signs, daily care, and help sought, all through that trip lens. The team took findings back to the group to plan next steps. Silcock and colleagues say care must be built with Pacific kin, not just sold to them.
plos-pone-0355489:
Leanna Silva Aquino and co-authors probed health care access in Quilombola towns in the Santarém part of the Brazilian Amazon. Quilombola towns were founded by Afro-Brazilian forebears who fled slavery. Brazil vows care for all, but rivers, miles, and want ration it in fact. Their 2026 survey asked five hundred twelve adults in nine rural and riverside towns.

Five forecast models, from tree-based to shrunk regressions, were ranked on how well they foresaw self-reported access. Layered models and part-picking tools split the roles of self, clinic, and land. Aquino and colleagues pair machine learning with plain stats to show which walls bind most, so policy can aim at Amazon facts, not state-wide means.
plos-pone-0355389:
Kittipan Tharakhet and colleagues test in 2026 a messenger RNA vaccine in mice aimed at all four types of dengue virus at once. Four distinct types make dengue hard to vaccinate against, since protection must cover each one. Their design blends parts of a viral protein from every type into one shared version, packed into tiny fat droplets for delivery.

Even a low dose raised antibodies that recognised the protein from all four types. Immune cells also reacted to pieces from several types, though each single type response was weaker than a focused vaccine might give. The authors see the shared design as a useful addition to future dengue vaccines.
plos-pone-0355289:
Perpetual Arthur and co-authors interview in 2026 traditional medicine practitioners in Ghana who often see women first with breast concerns. These healers work outside formal services yet hold strong community trust. Talks explored how they learned their craft, what they believe causes breast cancer, which signs they watch for, and how they judge a case.

Healers mixed inherited knowledge with workshops and some contact with formal medicine, and they named key signs such as lumps and nipple changes. False beliefs about spiritual causes and reliance on feel and intuition risked missed or wrong calls. Training and referral links could turn their reach into earlier detection, the authors argue.
plos-pone-0350289:
Aimee Haley, Alebachew Haybano, and Gun-Britt Wärvik outline in 2026 a review plan mapping research on what happens to doctoral graduates' careers in Africa. Little joined up evidence exists on whether graduates stay in universities or move elsewhere, and what helps or blocks each path. Four databases were searched for English peer reviewed work with no year limit.

Screening against set criteria will sort which studies count, and charting will cover theories used, methods used, and how far non academic careers appear. Conditions at system, institution, and personal levels are a special focus. University leaders could use the map to build better career support and spot research gaps.
plos-pone-0341389:
Christine Prosperi and co-authors report in 2026 a pilot in Zambia testing whether leftover blood samples from district hospitals can track population immunity. Such samples are cheap and ready made compared with household surveys, though they may not mirror the whole population. Teams at three facilities in two districts collected leftover child and adult samples over several months to estimate measles protection.

Collection worked, yet the pilot showed changes needed for scale, above all tighter weaving into daily lab and hospital routines. The authors share design lessons and practical recommendations for other low resource settings that want rapid immunity estimates during outbreaks.
plos-pone-0354889:
Mohammed Kebede and five colleagues published this 2026 community study of parents in Dire Dawa, eastern Ethiopia, who treated their children with traditional medicine during COVID-19. Nearly a thousand parents answered surveys, and interviews explored how families learn, prepare, store, and dose herbal remedies, and why they hide that use from health workers.

Almost nine in ten parents had used traditional remedies for their children, usually alongside clinic medicine, and almost none told health staff, fearing blame. Kebede urges stronger traditional medicine policy and open conversation instead of silence that can endanger children.
plos-pone-0354689:
Ping Zou led a team of seven authors on this 2026 pharmacy study building a two-speed painkiller tablet. Ketorolac is a strong pain reliever whose effect fades fast, forcing frequent doses. Their tablet-in-tablet design wraps a slow-release core in a fast-dissolving outer layer, tuned through systematic formulation experiments.

The finished pill released about a third of its dose within half an hour for quick relief, then kept releasing past ninety percent over a full day. Zou presents the design as a practical way to stretch strong pain relief without extra pills.
plos-pone-0353489:
Francis Okyere and Michael Nyanney published this 2026 statistics study of breast cancer risk models built from tumor measures in a classic Wisconsin data set. They compared three penalized regression methods that shrink or drop predictors, judging not only accuracy but whether repeated samples keep choosing the same tumor features.

All three separated cancer from non-cancer almost perfectly, and more honest risk scores than plain regression. Ridge kept every feature steadily, lasso was sparse but jumpy, and elastic net balanced both. Okyere argues stability checks belong in medical prediction, not accuracy alone.
plos-pone-0354589:
Zuo and colleagues report a 2026 review of past cases of a rare, benign bone tumor in the upper arm of children. The tumor, called chondroblastoma, was treated at one center over ten years. Care used scraping out the tumor, heat treatment of the cavity walls, and packing the space with bone graft.

Seventeen young patients were followed for at least seven years after surgery. One child needed a second operation when the tumor came back. More than half saw the treated arm end up a bit shorter than the other, and this was more common in younger children. Even so, arm and shoulder function scores stayed good in both groups. The authors present the method as a sound option, while warning that return of the tumor and uneven growth remain real risks.
plos-pone-0347989:
Rees and colleagues, in a 2026 report, study how air filters were received in care homes during a large trial called AFRI-c. The trial tested whether high-grade filters that trap tiny particles could cut chest infections among residents. This companion study asked a different question: did people accept the machines, and were they used as intended?

Researchers spoke with staff, residents, and relatives across twenty-two homes, and gathered survey answers from many more. Filter use soon felt normal, though some residents disliked the draft from the machines. Homes reported keeping the filters on faithfully, and satisfaction with the home did not change. That matters because the main trial found no drop in infections. Strong use means the flat result cannot be blamed on poor follow-through. Staff prized infection control, while residents cared more about comfort and daily life.
plos-pone-0354489:
Nian and colleagues present a 2026 protocol for a review of what women should be allowed to eat and drink during labor. For decades, many hospitals kept laboring women fasting, fearing food might enter the lungs under anesthesia. Modern anesthesia has made that event rare, while fasting can leave women hungry, thirsty, and worn out. Guidelines now disagree.

The planned review will search a wide set of English and Chinese databases for trials that compare ways of managing oral intake in labor. A network method will rank the options against each other, even ones never tested head to head. Outcomes include how birth happens, newborn health scores and blood sugar, and mothers' comfort, thirst, and satisfaction. Two reviewers will screen and rate the studies separately. As a protocol, the paper sets out the plan and questions; the answers will come when the review itself is done.
plos-pone-0353689:
Liu and colleagues, in a 2026 study, untangle the two-way link between thinking ability and depressive symptoms in older British adults, with physical activity in the middle. Earlier work showed each can worsen the other, but not the order of events or the mechanism. The team used a national aging study that measured the same people three times across about five years.

Nearly seven thousand adults aged fifty and over took part. Thinking and mood each predicted the other at the next wave, in a negative loop: weaker thinking foretold worse mood, and worse mood foretold weaker thinking. Thinking was the stronger driver of the pair. Activity carried a small part of the effect: weaker thinking led to less activity, which then led to worse mood. The authors suggest that keeping older adults moving may soften one path from cognitive decline into depression.
plos-pone-0351989:
Kora Tushune Godana and seven colleagues review what holds back Ethiopia's community health programme, in this 2026 PLOS ONE scoping review. Since 2003, health extension workers have carried basic preventive care into villages across the country. The reviewers gathered studies, government reports, and partner documents to map the obstacles at every level of the system.

One deep tension stood out: the programme offers prevention, while communities ask for treatment, which erodes trust. The mostly female workforce faces barriers in some cultural settings, and training, retention, and digital skills all lag. The authors recommend adding basic curative services, balancing the workforce, and improving workers' conditions before expecting better results.
plos-pone-0352689:
George Allison and three colleagues automate a computer pipeline that estimates children's bone strength from CT scans, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. The existing method predicts how much bending a child's thigh bone can bear, useful in bone-fragility care, but demands a trained operator clicking through many steps. Their Python application automates the process, including the fiddly job of marking anatomical landmarks, and packages everything into one contained tool.

Scans of sixty-nine children ran through both the old and new pipelines. The automatic landmarks landed almost exactly where human ones did, the strength results matched published experiments, and the whole job finished in about thirteen minutes instead of thirty-five. Automation of this kind is what lets a research method serve whole clinic cohorts.
plos-pone-0352589:
Chiodi and colleagues studied wheat fields shaded by solar panels in a 2026 field study. Pairing panels with crops lets one field yield both food and power, but shade changes the soil below. The team compared open sun with two panel layouts, one covering a small share of ground and one covering a much larger share.

Soil under the wider layout held more carbon, nitrogen, and key minerals than soil in open sun or under the sparse layout. Microbe communities in the soil also shifted with panel cover at two points in the season. The results suggest panel spacing shapes soil health, not just crop yield, so farm designs should weigh both outcomes together.
plos-pone-0353789:
Shao, Gao, and Sun modeled greener delivery of fresh farm goods at varied temperatures in a 2026 study. Foods needing different cold levels often travel in separate trucks, wasting space and fuel. Their model plans routes and three-dimensional truck loading together, aiming to cut both cost and carbon output.

A hybrid search method mixing two classic techniques solved the plan efficiently. Tested on real data from a fresh goods supply firm, joint delivery cut running costs by about three tenths and carbon output by a similar share versus separate delivery. The savings show that sharing trucks across temperature needs can pay, when loading is planned with care.
plos-pone-0348789:
Batool and colleagues developed a protein-enriched fruit leather from quince and almond in a 2026 study. Fruit leather is a chewy, shelf-stable snack, usually rich in sugar but poor in protein. Five blends mixed quince pulp with rising shares of almond powder, then dried them with hot air.

Each blend was checked for nutrition, antioxidant power, and firmness when pulled. Almond adds protein and healthy fats to quince's fiber and antioxidants. The work targets snacks that travel well without refrigeration, useful for school and travel markets. Balancing taste, strength, and nutrition across blends guides which recipe deserves wider production trials.
plos-pone-0352089:
Touitou-Burckard and colleagues set out an expert consensus plan in 2026 on joined-up care for people with severe mental illness and physical disease. Such patients often fall between mental and physical services. Stakeholders from six European countries, including patients and relatives, will vote through up to three online rounds.

The aim is agreement on what good integrated care must include to last in real systems. Patients, families, clinicians, and officials rarely define best practice together, so this process builds the definition jointly. Agreed features can then guide services that treat mind and body in one plan rather than in competing silos.
plos-pone-0353189:
Kouchaki and colleagues tracked recovery after traumatic brain injury in a registry study in a 2026 paper. Nearly three thousand survivors were scored at hospital discharge and again six months later. Change was classed as recovering, stable, or slipping back, then linked to early clinical, lab, and scan factors.

Movement in both directions was common after discharge, so a single early score misleads. Some early factors predicted which path a patient would take, even within the same discharge score group. Families and rehab teams can plan better when likely paths are known, and follow-up visits can target those at risk of slipping back.
plos-pone-0352889:
Dan Feng Huang and Dennis Tay present this 2026 PLOS One study on the distinctive style of translated language, using speeches from United Nations meetings as their test case. Translated text carries subtle fingerprints that differ from originally written text, and earlier classifiers could spot them without explaining how. The authors built a deep learning framework designed to reveal its own reasoning through a perturbation method that tests which features drive its decisions.

Their model separated translated from non-translated texts with strong accuracy. More importantly, the explanation step showed the decisions rested on style patterns deeper than surface word choice or sentence structure. The authors offer the framework as a proof of concept for other language studies where researchers need to know not just what a model decides, but why.
plos-pone-0346089:
Takehiko Hanaki and five co-authors set out this 2026 PLOS One protocol for a systematic review. The review will test a glowing dye technique used during liver surgery. Bile leaking from the cut surface after liver removal causes infections and longer stays. It can also force repeat procedures. A fluorescent dye lets surgeons spot leaks during the operation and fix them on the spot. Study results on whether this prevents serious leaks are mixed.

As a protocol, the paper describes the plan. Four databases and trial registries will be searched. The review will name the outcomes that count. Randomized and non-randomized studies will be pooled apart and graded for certainty. No results are reported yet. The finished review should settle whether dye-guided leak checks deserve a routine place in liver surgery.
plos-pone-0351689:
Mika Allyssa Esquillo and seven colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One secondary analysis of guilt in sixty-one veterans with combat-related post-traumatic stress disorder enrolled in a clinical trial. The authors separated two kinds of guilt: guilt over one's own actions, and survivor guilt over living when others died, then tested how each relates to symptom severity and depression.

Both kinds of guilt independently predicted overall symptom severity. Action guilt alone predicted avoidance and emotional numbing, but that link ran substantially through depression, which carried part of its effect. The authors argue therapists should assess the two guilts separately, and that treating depression may be one route by which action guilt loosens its grip on the numbing symptoms of the disorder.
plos-pone-0351189:
Marzieh Asadi and colleagues designed, entirely on a computer, a new test ingredient for a worm infection called strongyloidiasis. The parasite Strongyloides stercoralis is most dangerous for people with weak immune systems, and current blood tests miss cases or give false alarms. A sharper test could help doctors find infections earlier.

The team picked the most telling pieces of four parasite proteins and joined them into one fusion protein, choosing parts that react strongly but do not cross-react with other germs. Computer checks covered its shape, stability, and how well bacteria could be made to produce it, and they prepared the gene code for a standard lab vector. Lab testing would be the next step beyond this design study.
plos-pone-0349889:
Francesca Bettio, Fernando Flores Tavares, and Elisa Ticci revisited a grim question from the pandemic: did violence between partners get worse under lockdown in Tuscany, Italy? They drew on a large phone survey run in twenty twenty-one, described as the only locally representative one of its kind in Italy. They also asked which pandemic shock mattered most, money trouble or being stuck at home.

Respondents said violence had, on balance, grown more frequent or more severe. Among the shocks, the strain of caring for children at home weighed heaviest, job loss came next, and crowding without privacy showed no clear effect. How violence was measured also changed the answers: a measure counting severity picked up effects a simple yes-or-no missed.
plos-pone-0352189:
Donath Valerian and colleagues swabbed the furniture and fittings of Tanzania's national cancer institute, hunting for two families of drug-resistant bacteria. Cancer patients stay long in hospital and have weakened defenses, so germs waiting on bed rails and keyboards are a real threat. Two hundred forty-seven samples came from six kinds of surfaces, from sinks to nursing station tables.

About one surface in twelve carried MRSA, the resistant staph germ, and about one in four carried bacteria that defeat a wide family of antibiotics. Two species dominated the second group, and some isolates resisted nearly every drug tested, though all staph still answered to one reserve antibiotic. For a hospital serving highly vulnerable patients, the findings turn routine deep cleaning and hand hygiene from housekeeping into treatment.
plos-pone-0331989:
Reva Mosleh and colleagues surveyed three hundred forty-six women attending two Beirut fertility centers about what they know, feel, and expect from assisted reproductive technology, the lab-based treatments for infertility. Lebanon had no such baseline. Interviewers worked through questionnaires on knowledge, attitudes, and expectations, then modeled what moves each score.

Just over half the women showed good knowledge and positive attitudes, while nearly three quarters held high expectations, a gap clinics should notice. Hearing about the treatments from a doctor lifted both knowledge and attitudes more than any other source. Older age trimmed expectations, and hormone disorders raised them. The authors argue for structured education inside fertility care and honest expectation-setting, since hope untethered from odds sets patients up for financial and emotional harm.
plos-pone-0349589:
Android malware keeps mutating and hiding its code, so Vu Minh Manh, Cho Do Xuan, and Nguyen Thi Khanh Van built a detector that reads an app two ways at once. Their 2026 PLOS One framework, HybFusion, fuses behavior traces with permission meanings.

One branch maps how the app's functions call each other, learning the shape of its behavior. The other reads the permissions the app requests as a sentence, catching suspicious combinations. A stacked team of classifiers then votes on the combined picture. Wide testing showed stronger detection and fewer false alarms than single-view rivals, which the authors credit to the two views covering each other's blind spots.
plos-pone-0349789:
Abdullah A Aljughaiman and colleagues traced how volatility shocks pass between Europes carbon trading market and stock markets in five emerging European economies. A quantile based model let shock strength differ in calm, falling, and booming conditions. Carbon price swings matter for firms that must buy pollution permits, so spillover strength guides portfolio choices.

Shocks ran far stronger in booming, high volatility states, where total connectedness neared ninety percent, versus about thirty percent in calm or falling states. Greece, Poland, and Hungary absorbed more carbon shocks, while Slovakia absorbed least in every state. Slovak shares thus act as a useful hedge when carbon markets turn wild, the authors suggest.
plos-pone-0344889:
Hammad Ur Rehman Bajwa, Suman Bhowmick, and Csaba Varga analysed one hundred and seventy seven multi state United States outbreaks of animal linked Salmonella from 2009 to 2022. Outbreak records from a national system were mapped as networks joining germ types, animal sources, settings, and states, while a learning model ranked which traits best distinguish outbreak profiles.

Rates fell from 2009 to 2013 then held steady. Birds and reptiles mattered most as sources, and feed stores and homes as settings. Two outbreak families emerged: bird linked farm and store outbreaks across central and eastern regions, and reptile and mammal linked home outbreaks. Backyard poultry guidance at feed stores is a prime prevention lever.
plos-pone-0350989:
Monalisa M J Faulkner and colleagues charted sickle cell disease in Sierra Leone from 1990 to 2023 in work published in 2026. The inherited blood disorder kills many African children, yet country level figures for this high burden nation were scarce.

Using global burden estimates, they tracked cases, deaths, and lost healthy years. Estimated cases nearly doubled over the period, and deaths rose too, even though the death rate for each age group fell. Population growth drove much of the rise. The split matters: clinics face more patients even as care slowly improves, so services must expand, not just improve.
plos-pone-0348589:
Jaida N Elcock and co-authors tracked basking sharks on their winter migration from the northwest Atlantic in 2026. These huge filter feeders summer off North America's northeast coast, then head for warm southern waters, and what they do on the way was largely unknown.

Satellite tags recorded depth and temperature each day. On the shelf the sharks stayed shallow, but offshore they dived through mid-depth water in a daily rhythm, rising and sinking with the layers where small prey gather and scatter. Their diving overlapped both prey layers. The behaviour suggests the migration is also a feeding journey, not just a move to warmth.
plos-pone-0350089:
Natalia Ioannou and Iliatha Papachristou Nadal interviewed midlife women in the United Kingdom living with type two diabetes in 2026. General studies blur how gender and life stage shape the illness, and midlife brings its own pile of roles and changes.

Thirteen women recruited through social media and a research panel spoke in depth online. Four themes covered the daily practical work of the condition, its emotional and social weight, its place in identity and relationships, and how women look ahead. The accounts show diabetes woven into work, family, and ageing, a fuller picture than blood sugar numbers alone give services.
plos-pone-0347789:
Lily Wright, Phoebe Barnett, and co-authors interviewed young people about Early Support Hubs, community services in parts of England offering open-access help for ages eleven to twenty-five without a referral. Youth mental health needs are high, but clinic waiting lists and strict entry thresholds leave many waiting. Their 2026 study spoke with twenty users, aged sixteen to twenty-five, across eight hub services.

Young people prized the hubs' easy access, their whole-person help beyond clinical treatment, and the sense of community and steady relationships they found there. They also named weaknesses: many locals had never heard of the hubs, the services could not handle the most severe needs, and their scale was small. The authors say hubs look like a valued partner to clinic services, but evidence on who they reach and what outcomes follow is still needed.
plos-pone-0337789:
Josphat Kosgei and Walter Jaoko led a study of two viruses that often meet in one body. The viruses are HIV and hepatitis B. They share routes of spread. The data came from a large cohort in Kenya, Uganda, Tanzania, and Nigeria. More than four thousand people at twelve clinics were tested. The team looked at who carried both viruses at once.

About five in a hundred people with HIV also had hepatitis B. The rate barely topped that of people with no HIV. Place and person mattered much more. Nigeria's rate passed eleven in a hundred, while Kenya's stayed under three. Men had twice the rate of women. The oldest adults were hit most. The team urges routine hepatitis B tests in HIV care.
plos-pone-0350389:
Mandy H M Chu, William K K Wu, and co-authors published a 2026 protocol for a phase two trial of taurine supplements in healthcare workers. Taurine, a nutrient the body makes in small amounts, falls with age in animal studies, and restoring it improved metabolic health in those experiments. The planned trial will randomly assign about eighty workers to daily taurine or an identical placebo for six months, with patients, staff, and assessors all blinded.

The main question is whether more participants on taurine see their long-term blood sugar marker fall at all over six months. Secondary measures include blood fats, blood pressure, weight, a biological age estimate, and a skin marker of sugar damage. The design checks results at intervals and can stop early for success or futility. Findings will decide whether a larger trial is justified.
plos-pone-0349689:
Anjana Maharjan and Shobha Laxmi Bajracharya surveyed one hundred twenty-nine caregivers at a Nepali teaching hospital who look after frail elderly relatives with mental disorders. Their 2026 study measured how caregivers cope and how heavy the burden feels, using Nepali versions of two standard questionnaires during face-to-face interviews.

Caregivers leaned on both problem-focused and emotion-focused coping. Nearly half reported little or no burden, but about fifteen percent felt a severe burden, split between personal strain and the strain of the role itself. Women, caregivers in nuclear families, and the employed carried significantly higher burden levels. Coping style and burden showed no firm statistical link, though problem-focused coping trended protective. The authors call for targeted counseling and support for the most pressed caregivers.
plos-pone-0331189:
Baojing Zhang and colleagues built a deep learning system that cleans up radar images used to measure ground movement around mines. Radar interferometry tracks sinking or shifting land, but the wrapped phase signal must be unwrapped before it means anything. Heavy mining deforms the ground so sharply that older methods often fail.

Their network, called MAPUNet, reads the radar pattern at several scales at once and pays extra attention to the most useful features while cutting noise. Tested on simulated images with strong gradients and heavy noise, it unwrapped the phase more accurately than standard approaches. Better unwrapping means more trustworthy warnings about ground movement in mining areas.
plos-pone-0334989:
Zijian Chen and colleagues built a computer vision model that spots diseases on tomato plants, work now usually done by slow hand inspection in the field. Diseased spots can be tiny, varied in size, and lost against messy backgrounds of leaves and soil. Their model, TDD-YOLO, upgrades a popular detection system with three changes aimed at exactly those problems.

One module sharpens the texture of faint disease spots, another helps the model link features across the image while ignoring background clutter, and a third handles spots at different scales. Precise, fast detection matters because catching an outbreak days earlier can save a harvest. Models like this are a step toward camera-based crop scouting on farms.
plos-pone-0347489:
Rodziah Romli and colleagues tested whether a short educational video could move Malaysian women in middle adulthood to get screened for cervical cancer. The video, called SeDAR, was built on a theory of protection motivation, addressing how vulnerable women feel, how serious the disease is, and how confident they feel about acting. Seventy-six women took part, half watching the video and half receiving a digital pamphlet.

Screening uptake, knowledge, and motivation were compared between the groups, with experts and users having vetted the video beforehand. Cervical cancer is preventable when screening catches early changes, yet uptake lags in many communities. A phone-friendly video that measurably beats a pamphlet would give clinics a cheap tool for closing that gap.
plos-pone-0348189:
Sung-Ha Kim and colleagues measured how South Korea's 2024 medical workforce crisis changed patient transfers at a hospital with a specialized children's emergency center. When the government expanded medical school admissions, most junior doctors walked out, and emergency departments nationwide were strained. The study compared the year before the policy with the year after, covering nearly ninety-eight thousand visits.

Transfers between hospitals, a sign a department cannot cope, were analyzed with time-series and adjusted statistical methods, separately for children and adults. The team also examined why transferred children moved and how long they stayed. Pediatric care needs dedicated staff and equipment, so children may suffer first in a workforce shock. Documenting that pattern is how systems learn to shield children's services next time.
plos-pone-0349289:
Jiaying Lan and colleagues surveyed four hundred twenty-five Taiwanese university students studying in mainland China about the strain between who they feel they are and how they appear to others. Identity gap theory separates mismatches between the self and its public performance, its relationships, and its group memberships. Studying within a shared broader culture, rather than across East and West, tests whether these gaps still matter.

The survey measured all three gap types and how well students were adapting psychologically. With student flows inside Asia rising fast, this intra-cultural movement is understudied compared with the classic move to Western universities. Identifying which identity gap tracks adaptation most closely tells universities where counseling and community support will do the most good for mobile students.
plos-pone-0349389:
Diana Yaneth Vargas and Fred Russell Kramer describe a lab test that can tell whether two mutations in the same gene sit on the same copy of a chromosome. It can also tell when they sit on opposite copies. That detail matters in lung cancer care, because a second change in a gene can make a targeted drug stop working. Their method uses two specially designed primers that only multiply DNA when both changes are present together on one strand.

Working with two well-known changes in the EGFR gene, the team showed the test stays silent when only one change is present or when the changes sit apart. The test is sensitive enough to guide an early switch to a better drug, and it can run on DNA from a simple blood sample using common lab machines.
plos-pone-0349089:
Xinjie Wang and colleagues isolated a new virus that hunts Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a bacterium behind severe lung, blood, and eye infections that shrugs off many antibiotics. Three candidate viruses were collected around a campus. One, named PW01, was characterised in depth. The team checked which clinical strains it attacks, how it grows, and whether it wrecks the protective biofilms the bacteria build. They also read what its genome says about its lifestyle.

The virus attacked a broad range of strains, suppressed growth in dishes, and tore into established biofilms, while its genome confirmed a strictly lethal style with no lurking phase. In infected mouse wounds, the virus combined with antibiotics cleared more bacteria than either alone. The authors back pairing phage with antibiotics as a practical strategy against drug-resistant infections.
plos-pone-0348889:
Marco Helbich and co-workers set out a plan to learn how the streets people walk actually shape their walking habits. Moving too little harms health, and poorer groups are hit hardest. Their 2026 protocol describes a study in Amsterdam that will follow about two hundred adults with phones tracking movement and steps for a week.

Walk-along interviews will capture how streets feel on foot, while computer vision reads features from street photos. The team also plans a smart tool that suggests place-based fixes, such as greener or safer routes. As a protocol, the paper reports no results yet. Its design aims to move past simple surveys toward what walkers truly meet outdoors.
plos-pone-0342889:
Peng Ge and co-workers study how heat changes the dissolved organic matter that coal leaves in mine water. Such matter could fingerprint where mine water comes from, but deep mines run hot and heat may rewrite the fingerprint. Their 2026 study warms extracts from three coal grades in the lab and reads their molecules with an ultra-fine mass tool, guided by machine learning.

Warming broke down and oxidized matter from young coals, spreading their variety. In the oldest coal grade, heat instead concentrated dense, sulfur-rich structures into a stable, distinct signature. A few molecular traits predicted how reactive each sample would be. Refined fingerprints could help engineers trace dangerous water rushes in deep mines before they flood workings.
plos-pone-0348289:
Wen Qin and co-workers test how the tone of a place's revival policy affects whether tourists want to visit. Governments issue such policies to breathe life back into fading destinations. Their 2026 paper runs seven studies, from interviews to scenario experiments, splitting policies into flexible ones that feel warm and personal and rigid ones that feel strict and official.

Flexible policies generally sparked stronger travel intentions. They did so by making the destination feel warm, while rigid policies made it feel competent instead. Timing flipped the advice: flexible tones worked better for trips coming soon, rigid tones for trips planned far ahead. Marketers can match policy wording to how far off the trip sits in a traveler's mind.
plos-pone-0341789:
Saleh A. Alghamdi asked three hundred seventy-nine Saudi adults about hard times in youth and rash acts as grown-ups. Women told of more hard times than men. The gaps sat in two spots: being left cold by kin, and sick minds in the home. His study used strict checks to keep false hits out.

Once those checks were in, men and women scored the same on all rash act scales. Hard times tied to more rash acts in women than in men at first glance. But firm tests showed that gap was not real. The true split is how much harm each sex met, not how weak each is. Aid should fit the type of harm, for all.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Cambodia brought a border complaint to the Council in 1964. South Viet Nam's troops had crossed into its land, and people had died. Resolution 189, passed by all members on 4 June 1964, is the reply. Cambodia had asked the Council to name the wrong and stop it.

The Council deplored the raids. It said fair payment should be made to Cambodia for the harm done. It asked all states to respect Cambodia's borders and its neutral stance. It also sent three of its own members to both lands and to the sites of the attacks. They had to report back in forty-five days with ways to stop a repeat.

On 13 August 2003, by a full vote, the Council took up a hard case. It deals with the probe into the theft of Congo's wealth. A team of experts had told the Council in July that the looting went on, most of all in the east. This theft fed the trade in small arms and kept the war alive. A new joint government had just formed in the capital.

The Council backed the team's work to the end. The team was in talks with named firms, men, and states, and their replies were printed with its report. The team had to clear up who did what and bring its facts up to date. Its term was thus stretched to let it finish.

Resolution 1889, passed on 5 October 2009, takes up the cause of women in war and peace. Nine years before, a landmark text had called for women to have a real say in peace talks and postwar plans. This text backs that call in full. It also backs later texts on rape as a weapon of war and on children in war. A UN report of September 2009 took stock of the gains made so far.

The gains, the Council found, were too slow. Its reply was to count what counts. It set in train a set of clear marks to track how the 2000 pledge is kept across the world. It asked for fresh reports on women's share in peace work and postwar planning. What gets counted, the thought ran, gets done.

East Timor's invasion is answered in Resolution 389, adopted on 22 April 1976 by twelve votes to none with two abstentions. Indonesia had sent forces into the Portuguese colony the previous December, days after a local party declared independence. The Council's earlier resolution of December 1975 had demanded withdrawal; the Secretary-General's special envoy had been consulting the parties since.

The Council called on all states to respect East Timor's territorial integrity and its people's right to self-determination. It called on Indonesia to withdraw all its forces from the territory without further delay. And it asked the special representative to continue his mission and report back. Indonesia stayed for twenty-four years, but the UN never recognized the annexation.

On 16 January 2002, by a full vote, the Council passed Resolution 1389. It backs Sierra Leone's shift from war to the ballot box. The peace had moved well by then. The laying down of arms had just been declared done. The Council called for stray guns to be picked up from townsfolk and ex-fighters. It asked for sound funds for the scheme that brings ex-fighters back to civil life.

Free and fair votes, open to all, were named the base of long calm. The state and its vote board had made good strides, with UN help. All sides must be free to seek votes and to reach the press, the Council said. Sierra Leone's own police held the first duty for safety at the polls.

Afghanistan after its 2004 presidential vote is the setting for Resolution 1589, adopted on 24 March 2005. The UN Assistance Mission in Afghanistan, UNAMA, was due for renewal. Parliamentary votes were now set for 18 September 2005. Big tasks remained: fighting the drug trade, disarming militia forces, building state offices, and fixing the justice system.

The Council extends UNAMA for twelve more months. It urges fast work on a fair framework for the coming elections and asks donors to fund them promptly. It welcomes real gains in disarming and reintegrating fighters and pushes for the job to finish by June 2006. It backs the government's 2005 counter-narcotics plan and asks UNAMA to keep supporting fair courts, prison reform, and full respect for human rights, above all for women.

Cyprus faces a window of opportunity in Resolution 1789, adopted on 14 December 2007. The island stayed stable, with fewer incidents along the Green Line. The 8 July 2006 Agreement was still not implemented, and public debate about the island's future was narrowing. EU money was agreed for demining of the buffer zone.

The Council declares the status quo unacceptable and extends the UN Peacekeeping Force in Cyprus, UNFICYP, until 15 June 2008. It voices concern at the lack of progress and tells all parties to engage with UN efforts, stop mutual recriminations, and show flexibility so progress can open the way to full negotiations. It urges talks with UNFICYP on marking the buffer zone, including the Ledra Street crossing. It again asks the Turkish Cypriot side and Turkish forces to restore the earlier position at Strovilia. A report is due by 1 June 2008.

Cyprus's peacekeeping force is extended while settlement talks stall in Resolution 2089, adopted on 24 January 2013. Negotiations had made progress but not enough for a comprehensive settlement. The Government of Cyprus agreed UNFICYP should stay past 31 January 2013. Access to the remaining buffer-zone minefields was still withheld.

The Council extends the United Nations Peacekeeping Force in Cyprus, UNFICYP, until 31 July 2013. It urges both leaders toward decisive progress on the core issues toward a bicommunal, bizonal federation with political equality. It calls the status quo unsustainable. It demands island-wide access for the Committee on Missing Persons. It calls on the Turkish Cypriot side and Turkish forces to restore the military status quo in Strovilia as it stood before 30 June 2000. It presses for demining access inside and beyond the buffer zone. It sets a further report by 10 July 2013.

The Great Lakes peace framework is recommitted in Resolution 2389, adopted in late 2017. Displacement across the region had passed 7 million internally displaced people and 3.5 million refugees. Armed groups still destabilized eastern Congo. The signatories of the Peace, Security and Cooperation Framework had renewed their commitment at Brazzaville on 19 October 2017.

The Council reaffirms the Framework as the essential mechanism for peace. It demands that all armed groups in Congo, including the FDLR, the ADF, and the LRA, cease violence at once, disband permanently, and demobilize the children in their ranks. Signatory states must neither support armed groups nor harbour war criminals. They must complete the repatriation of disarmed FDLR and former M23 combatants without precondition. Congo, backed by MONUSCO joint operations under Resolution 2348 (2017), must vigorously neutralize the remaining armed groups while protecting civilians. It must make progress on security sector reform and state authority.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly Resolution 1889 (XVIII), adopted on 6 November 1963, pressed Britain once more on Southern Rhodesia. The Assembly approved its Special Committee's report. It restated the people's right to self-rule and freedom. It voiced deep regret that Britain had not acted on the chain of earlier resolutions about the territory.

The minority government in the colony had asked Britain for independence under the 1961 constitution. The Assembly told Britain to refuse until majority rule based on a vote for every adult was in place. It told Britain to call a conference of all parties at once. The conference was to plan independence on that footing.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Security Council resolution 1189, adopted in 1998, responds to the terrorist bomb attacks of 7 August 1998 in Nairobi, Kenya, and Dar es Salaam, Tanzania. The Council strongly condemns the attacks, which killed hundreds of people, injured thousands and caused massive destruction, and expresses its deep sorrow and condolences to the victims' families.

The Council calls on all states and international institutions to support the investigations under way in Kenya, Tanzania and the United States. That support is so the perpetrators are caught and brought swiftly to justice. It thanks those who answered Kenyan and Tanzanian requests for help. It urges further assistance with reconstruction and disaster preparedness. It calls on every state, as a priority, to adopt practical measures against terrorism. Those measures are for the prosecution and punishment of those responsible.

Security Council resolution 1289, adopted on 7 February 2000, expands UNAMSIL, the United Nations Mission in Sierra Leone, as the West African force ECOMOG prepares to withdraw. The Council notes that UNAMSIL's deployment under resolution 1270 (1999) is nearly complete. It thanks ECOMOG for restoring security. It worries that disarmament is sporadic, abductees and child soldiers remain unreleased, and aid workers are still being attacked.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council raises UNAMSIL's military component to a maximum of 11,100 personnel. It adds tasks: guarding key sites in Freetown and Lungi airport, keeping supply routes open, and securing disarmament sites. The tasks include guarding collected weapons and protecting civilians under imminent threat of violence. The revised mandate runs six months. Reports come from the Secretary-General every 45 days. Troop levels can then be reviewed against conditions on the ground.

Liberia's timber ban is allowed to lapse in this text of 20 June 2006, easing the sanctions. Liberia's elected government, in office since January 2006, had reformed the forestry sector, cancelling all existing forest concessions and promising open management of timber income. The former president had also been transferred to the Special Court for Sierra Leone to face trial.

The timber measure is not renewed, though that choice would be reviewed after three months. Liberia is urged to pass the proposed forestry law quickly so the reforms will hold. The expert panel on Liberia is renewed for six more months to keep watching the remaining sanctions, which cover arms and diamonds, and the government's progress against the Council's conditions.

Guinea came under armed attack from outside forces in November 1970, and its president asked the United Nations for help. Guinea's representative told the Council that foreign troops and mercenaries had struck the country. The Council adopted Resolution 289 unanimously on 23 November 1970, the day after the attack began.

The Council demanded an immediate end to the armed attack. All external armed forces and mercenaries had to withdraw at once. The military equipment used in the attack had to go with them. The Council also decided to send a special mission to Guinea. The mission would report on the situation right away. Its membership was to be settled between the Council's president and the Secretary-General, and the matter stayed on the Council's agenda.

A Pacific island nation sought a seat at the United Nations in 1981, a year after its independence. Resolution 489, adopted unanimously on 8 July 1981, deals with the application of the Republic of Vanuatu. The Council examined the application. It then recommended to the General Assembly that Vanuatu be admitted to membership in the United Nations. That single recommendation is the whole text of the resolution.

Complaints under the armistice agreements of 1949 filled the Council's agenda in November 1950. Those agreements had ended the fighting between Israel and its Arab neighbors. Egypt, Israel, and Jordan had all brought grievances. The chief of staff of the Truce Supervision Organization had reported on them. Resolution 89 was adopted on 17 November 1950.

The Council told the parties to route their complaints through the Mixed Armistice Commissions. Those joint bodies had been set up by the agreements themselves. One complaint needed urgent attention. Egypt said that thousands of Palestinian Arabs had been expelled. Any Arab whom the commission found entitled to return had to be let back. The text also banned moving people across borders or armistice lines without consulting the commissions first. The chief of staff had to report to the Council within ninety days.

Judges for the new war crimes court for Rwanda were being chosen in the spring of 1995. Governments had sent in nominations for the bench. Under the court's statute, the Security Council builds the list of candidates from those names. The General Assembly then elects the judges from the list. Resolution 989 was adopted unanimously on 24 April 1995.

The Council established a list of twelve candidates. Only nominations received by the Secretary-General before 7 April 1995 were considered. The names came from countries in Africa, Europe, Asia, and the Caribbean. The list would go to the General Assembly, which would elect the court's first judges from it. The step looks small on paper. In fact, it staffed the court that would try the organizers of the 1994 genocide in Rwanda.
un-sc-res-189:
Cambodia charged South Vietnam with raids across its border in 1964. Saigon's troops had crossed into Cambodian land. People had died in the raids. Saigon's government said it was sorry for them. On 4 June 1964 the Council deplored the raids. It took note of the regrets. Both states, it noted, wanted their ties back to normal.

Fair payment had to be made to Cambodia for the harm done. Those at fault had to act to stop more raids. All states had to respect Cambodia's neutral stance and its borders. The vote passed with no one against. Raids tied to the Vietnam War kept troubling Cambodia for years.
un-sc-res-1489:
The looting of Congo's mineral wealth kept an expert panel in place under a Council decision of 13 August 2003. The panel's chairman had told the Council in July that the plunder went on, above all in the east of the Democratic Republic of the Congo. A transitional government had just taken office in Kinshasa.

The Council asked the Secretary-General to extend the Expert Panel's mandate. It repeated its demand that all states act at once to stop the illegal taking of Congo's resources. The panel would share its information with the governments concerned. Parties that settled their cases could be struck from its annexes. The Council stressed the link between resource theft and the small arms trade that kept the eastern war alive. This hosted file carries the same text as resolution 1499, adopted at the same meeting.
un-sc-res-1889:
Women's part in peace and security was pushed forward on 5 October 2009. The Council restated its line of texts from resolution 1325 (2000) through 1888 (2009). It had the Secretary-General's report of 16 September 2009 before it. It praised states that had drawn up national action plans under resolution 1325 and urged more of the same.

The Council urged member states and regional bodies to raise women's roles at every stage of peace work. It restated its call for all parties in armed conflict to respect the law that protects women and girls, and it condemned every breach of that law. The Secretary-General was asked to build a strategy to raise the number of women in decision posts on peace and security. His country reports had to carry data on women in armed conflict.
un-sc-res-389:
East Timor's occupation was challenged again on 22 April 1976. The Council recalled resolution 384 (1975) and had the Secretary-General's report of 12 March 1976. East Timorese spokesmen had addressed it. Indonesia's forces, which had entered the territory the previous December, remained in place. The question also sat before the General Assembly.

The Council called on all states to respect East Timor's territorial integrity. It restated the people's right to self-determination under the 1960 declaration on self-rule. Indonesia was called to withdraw all its forces from East Timor without further delay. The Secretary-General's special representative was to continue the task set under resolution 384 and keep consulting the parties. He also had to report on the text's progress as soon as possible. All states were asked to help the United Nations win a peaceful solution and finish freeing the territory.
un-sc-res-1389:
Sierra Leone's coming elections were written into UNAMSIL's tasks on 16 January 2002. Disarmament had officially ended, and the peace process was advancing. The electoral commission had asked the United Nations for support. Free, fair, and open elections were judged key to the country's long-term stability. The Secretary-General's report of 13 December 2001 set out the needs.

The Council decided that UNAMSIL would help the smooth holding of the elections. Its Chapter VII powers under resolution 1270 (1999) were restated. The mission's civilian police element would grow as the Secretary-General had proposed. An interim electoral section inside UNAMSIL was welcomed, with offices planned in each electoral district. The mission's public information work for the electoral commission drew praise. The Council underlined that Sierra Leone's government and commission bore the prime duty for free and fair polls, and it urged help for voters and parties alike.
un-sc-res-1589:
UNAMA was renewed after Afghanistan's first presidential vote on 24 March 2005. The presidential election of 9 October 2004 had been held with success. Parliamentary and local elections now had to be prepared. Narcotics, weak security in some regions, terror threats, and illegal armed groups all pressed at once. The Secretary-General's report of 18 March guided the renewal.

The Council extended UNAMA's mandate for twelve more months. It praised the United Nations' work beside the Afghan government and people. A framework for the mission's work with Kabul had to be set urgently, the Council stressed. Security for credible parliamentary, provincial, and district elections was named vital. The Council welcomed the world's help in setting up the new Afghan parliament. Substantial progress in disarming the militia forces was greeted. Kabul's fight against the drug trade won backing, with a call for stronger action by all states.
un-sc-res-1789:
In a vote on 14 December 2007, the Council passed Resolution 1789 on Cyprus. The island remained divided, and the peace process had yet to restart in full. The United Nations Peacekeeping Force in Cyprus, called UNFICYP, had patrolled the buffer zone since 1964.

The text extends the mandate of UNFICYP until 15 June 2008. It keeps faith with the goal of a bicommunal, bizonal federation with political equality. Both sides are urged to move from groundwork into full negotiations without more delay. The Council repeats its call to restore the past military position at Strovilia, as in earlier votes on Cyprus.
un-sc-res-2389:
The Great Lakes region was the matter before the Council in Resolution 2389, adopted on 8 December 2017. Displacement had passed ten million people across the region. Armed groups in eastern Congo still drew money from stolen minerals and wildlife. The 2013 peace framework for the region had won fresh pledges that October in Brazzaville.

The Council demands that all armed groups stop fighting at once. The FDLR, the ADF, and the LRA must disband, disarm, and free every child in their ranks. Ex-M23 and disarmed FDLR fighters should be sent home without conditions. States must not shelter war criminals or back armed groups in any form. Congo should press on with army reform and rebuild state authority in the east.
europmc-pmc10016089:
Reyes and a global team report a prospective cohort study of drug-resistant Pseudomonas infections in a 2023 paper. The germ in question resists carbapenems, a key class of antibiotics. Such infections form a worldwide threat, yet the spread and impact of the enzymes behind the resistance were unclear.

The study followed patients at hospitals in many countries and recorded their traits and outcomes. It also mapped how often each resistance enzyme appeared across regions. The findings give doctors and health planners a firmer picture of a hard-to-treat infection. They also guide the choice of antibiotics in hard cases.
europmc-pmc10144389:
Desai and colleagues review chitosan, a natural polymer with promise for drug delivery and medical use, in a 2023 paper. Chitosan comes from chitin, the material in crab and shrimp shells. It is safe in the body, breaks down naturally, and can be shaped into gels, films, and tiny carriers.

The review covers how chitosan is extracted and how each method changes its properties. It surveys uses in wound care, drug release, and tissue repair. The authors also note quality and safety questions. The paper maps a cheap, green material's path into medicine.
europmc-pmc10507089:
Borges do Nascimento and co-authors pooled reviews in 2023 on what helps or blocks digital health tools at work. Digital tools now touch most parts of care, from records to remote visits. The team searched five data banks for past reviews on barriers and aids. They kept 108 reviews that covered doctors, pharmacists, and nurses.

Weak networks and tech faults were the most cited barrier, Borges do Nascimento reports. Staff also feared more work hours and felt personal strain with new systems. Training and teaching plans stood out as a top aid. Rewards shared across sectors helped too. Staff who saw a tool as useful were far more apt to adopt it.
europmc-pmc10898089:
Astashyn and a large team present a fast screen for stray DNA in genome data in this 2024 paper. Genome assemblies, meaning full DNA readouts of a species, are being produced at a rapid pace. Stray DNA from other species can slip into these files and mislead research. The screen, called FCS-GX, is part of a toolkit from a US national data centre.

The tool scans most genomes in under ten minutes, the authors report. Tests on doctored genomes showed it catches diverse stray species with high accuracy. The team screened 1.6 million public assemblies and found 36.8 billion letters of stray DNA. Half of that came from just 161 files. Cleaned reference genomes then dropped to a tiny share of stray content. The tool is shared freely for labs to use.
europmc-pmc11344989:
Zhang and colleagues review Alzheimer disease mechanisms, trials, and new drug strategies in this 2024 paper. Alzheimer disease is the predominant form of dementia and a growing global challenge. Its causes mix ageing, genetics, and environment. Current theories include the amyloid and tau protein hypotheses, inflammation, oxidative stress, and faulty cell clean-up, among others.

Most clinical drugs of past decades were dropped for weak effect or adverse effects, the authors note. Available drugs mainly relieve symptoms and carry side effects of their own. Two antibodies, aducanumab and lecanemab, won US approval with potential disease-modifying effects. Their long-term efficacy and safety still need validation. The review maps how the many pathological theories interlock. It closes with the hunt for safer, more effective drugs and the open question of which process starts the disease.
europmc-pmc11468589:
van der Koog, Gandek, and Nagelkerke compare two drug delivery systems head to head in this 2022 review. Liposomes are artificial spherical vesicles made of lipid bilayers, the same fat sheets that form cell membranes. They can carry both water-loving and fat-loving cargo. Extracellular vesicles are natural particles secreted by cells and are more complex and body-friendly.

The review evaluates how the two systems differ and match in composition. Critical factors governing pharmacokinetics, meaning how long a carrier circulates and where it goes, are elucidated. Strategies to tweak circulation time, targeting, and cargo release into cells are explored for both. The authors detail the effects of each modification. They close by asking whether a hybrid, built only from the critical parts of each, could offer the best of both worlds.
europmc-pmc1182689:
Turner, Hahn, and Nuzhdin studied the African malaria mosquito in 2005. The species lives as two forms, called M and S. Both forms share the same places yet rarely interbreed. That split makes them a good case for studying how new species form.

Genome scans found just three regions where the forms truly differ. Two regions sit near chromosome centers and hold dozens of genes. The third region holds only five genes. Turner argues these small islands may keep the forms apart. The result shapes how scientists think about species in the making.
europmc-pmc1183189:
Kim and Volsky presented a 2005 method named PAGE for gene data. Labs often test thousands of genes at once on small chips. Single gene changes can look weak or noisy. Grouping genes into known sets gives a clearer signal of change.

PAGE uses standard math on those gene groups instead of slow shuffling tests. In trials it found more truly changed groups than the older method. It also ran much faster. Kim tested it on muscle data from young and old donors. Shared aging themes stood out more clearly at group level.
europmc-pmc1247189:
Armstrong, Hutchinson, Unwin, and Fletcher pooled studies on hydrocarbons and lung cancer in 2004. Hydrocarbon mixtures from work settings are known lung carcinogens. How risk climbs with dose was less clear. Thirty-nine worker cohorts entered the combined analysis.

At a set exposure unit, relative risk averaged 1.20, and that estimate held steady across methods and single studies. Coke ovens, gasworks, and aluminum plants clustered near 1.15 to 1.17, while other trades ran higher. Asphalt work and chimney sweeping showed far higher, though rougher, estimates.
