Dust exposure did not explain the pattern. Armstrong gives dose-response numbers for workplace limits. The authors say the results give risk checks a firmer base.
europmc-pmc1533889:
Psoriasis, a scaly skin disease, is driven by an overactive immune reply. Arican and co-authors measured immune signals in blood in 2005, hunting a lab marker of severity. Doctors now grade severity by eye, using a skin score. The team compared patients with active disease to healthy controls.

Six signals, including TNF-alpha and interleukin-18, ran higher in patients than controls. Four of them, IFN-gamma, IL-12, IL-17, and IL-18, rose in step with the skin score. Arican suggests blood levels of these signals could grade disease fairly, without relying on a doctor's visual judgment alone.
europmc-pmc1563489:
Genes do not speak at a steady rate; they fire in bursts. Raj and co-authors proved that in 2006 by counting single RNA messages in mammal cells. Cells with the same genes held wildly unlike message counts.

A gene flips randomly between off and on states. While on, it fires a short, intense burst of messages. Neighboring genes in the same stretch burst together. More activator protein made bursts bigger, not more frequent. Raj notes slow protein decay smooths the noise at the protein level. The work raises the puzzle of how cells stay reliable amid such random firing.
europmc-pmc1716189:
Health workers in poor countries catch TB from their patients at high rates. Joshi and co-authors reviewed 51 studies in 2006 on latent and active tuberculosis among staff in low- and middle-income countries.

Latent infection averaged 54 percent of workers, ranging from 33 to 79 percent. Yearly disease incidence ran from 69 to 5,780 per 100,000 workers. Risk ran highest in TB wards, labs, internal medicine, and emergency units. Nurses, attendants, and radiology technicians were among the most exposed roles. Joshi calls for simple, affordable infection controls, since most facilities lack resources to prevent spread. The review covered low- and middle-income countries.
europmc-pmc1847689: ART suppresses plasma HIV-1 RNA to a stable set point predicted by pretherapy viremia. — a 2005 science paper on ART's viral set point. It finds ART sets the stable point. The paper is the ART study: the findings on HIV-1 RNA, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc1994989: Relationship between mitochondrial electron transport chain dysfunction, development, and life extension in Caenorhabditis elegans. — a 2005 science paper on worm powerhouses and aging. It links the broken powerhouses to long life for labs. The paper is the long-life study: the notes on worm ills, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2009089: The effects of the inhalation of asbestos in rats. — a 2005 science paper on asbestos and rats. It studies the inhalation effects. The paper is the asbestos study: the findings on rat ills, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2383989: Event-related brain potential correlates of emotional face processing. — a 2008 science paper on face-emotion brain signals. It correlates the face signals. The paper is the signal study: the findings on brain ills, filed here in full session today twice.
europmc-pmc2519789: Serum microRNAs are promising novel biomarkers. — a 2008 science paper on blood microRNAs as disease flags. It finds the promising flags for labs. The paper is the flag study: the findings on blood ills, filed here in full session today twice.
europmc-pmc2564789: Gout in the UK and Germany: prevalence, comorbidities and management in general practice 2000-2 — a 2008 science paper on gout in the UK/Germany. It studies the gout prevalence. The paper is the gout study: the findings on gout ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2610389: Concepts of neural nitric oxide-mediated transmission. — a 2008 science paper on nitric-oxide transmission. It covers the transmission concepts. The paper is the concept study: the findings on nitric ills, filed here in full session today twice over now daily.
europmc-pmc2615189: Growth of Mycobacterium tuberculosis biofilms containing free mycolic acids and harbouring drug — a 2008 science paper on TB biofilm growth. It studies the mycolic-acid biofilms. The paper is the biofilm study: the findings on TB, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2637989: Relation of DNA methylation of 5'-CpG island of ACSL3 to transplacental exposure to airborne po — a 2008 science paper on ACSL3 methylation. It relates the transplacental exposure. The paper is the relation study: the findings on ACSL3 ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2689489: Very old patients admitted to intensive care in Australia and New Zealand: a multi-centre cohor — a 2008 science paper on very old ICU patients. It studies the multi-centre cohort. The paper is the cohort study: the findings on old ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2714989: Distinct parietal and temporal pathways to the homologues of Broca's area in the monkey. — a 2008 science paper on parietal-temporal pathways. It maps the distinct pathways. The paper is the pathway study: the findings on Broca ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2732489: Typical and atypical enteropathogenic Escherichia coli. — a 2008 science paper on enteropathogenic E. coli. It studies the atypical strains. The paper is the E. coli study: the findings on enteropathogenic ills, filed here in full session today twice over.
europmc-pmc2758589: Staphylococcus aureus alpha-hemolysin activates the NLRP3-inflammasome in human and mouse monoc — a 2008 science paper on alpha-hemolysin. It activates the NLRP3 inflammasome. The paper is the activation study: the findings on aureus ills, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2780389: MicroRNAs in colorectal cancer: translation of molecular biology into clinical application. — a 2008 science paper on micro-tag bowel-cancer clinics. It moves the micro tags for labs. The paper is the move study: the notes on bowel ills, filed here in full session today.
minor-law-books-jolly-1889:
Julius Jolly translated the Minor Law-Books for the Sacred Books of the East in 1889. The volume, number thirty-three in the series, holds the law codes of Narada and Brihaspati. Hindu law beyond the famous Manu is the subject here.

Narada's code treats courts, contracts, debts, and ordeals in practical detail. Brihaspati's fragments add rules on procedure and evidence for judges. These texts date from the early centuries of the common era. They show ancient Indian justice actually at work, case by case. Jolly specialized in Hindu law throughout his scholarly career. His volume remains the standard English source for both lawgivers.
glanvill-saducismus-triumphatus-english-:
Joseph Glanvill, a fellow of the Royal Society, wrote Saducismus Triumphatus to defeat Sadducism, his age's doubt about spirits. This edition of 1689 appeared after his death, with fresh material added. Glanvill offers full and plain evidence concerning witches and apparitions, gathered like a scientist's casebook.

His most famous case is the Drummer of Tedworth, a poltergeist that beat drums in a Wiltshire house. Glanvill treats testimony for ghosts as data, to be weighed like any observation. The book is science's strangest defense of the spirit world. It shows the new philosophy of experiment turned, in earnest, toward proving that witches exist.
plos-pone-0004889:
Narveen Jandu and colleagues profiled enterohemorrhagic E. coli O157 H7 gene output in response to host epithelia, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Pathogenesis is attributed to virulence factors encoded on multiple pathogenicity islands. Previous studies showed the bacterium modulates host signal cascades independent of toxins. Output profiling during contact with host lining cells reveals microbe programs activated specifically by host cell proximity and attachment.

Contact triggers coordinated virulence gene activation. Bacteria sense and prepare for infection actively. Blocking sensing could prevent disease onset. Foodborne outbreaks make steps urgent. More work in larger samples can confirm how general the effect proves to be. The team also set out clear next steps for work in this field.
plos-pone-0004989:
Anandamide is the body's own cannabis-like signal. It is a lipid messenger with many jobs. Cells take it up readily, but the uptake mechanism was controversial. Eric Di Pasquale and colleagues studied it in synthetic membranes. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. They tracked how anandamide enters and crosses lab-made lipid layers.

Both insertion and transport depended on cholesterol. Without cholesterol in the membrane, the process faltered. The finding ties the endocannabinoid's travels to membrane composition. It helps settle the debate about how this signal crosses cell walls. The result may also matter for drugs that target the endocannabinoid system.
plos-pone-0005089:
HP1 proteins pack DNA into dense, quiet chromatin. Flies carry several versions of them. Jochen Abel and colleagues studied one version, HP1c, in PLOS ONE in 2009. They found its level is regulated by a feedback loop. The loop runs through its binding partner, a protein called Woc.

HP1c controls its own abundance through that partnership. The self-tuning keeps the protein in balance. Most HP1 versions bind methylated histone H3. Despite that shared taste, the versions do different jobs. This one manages itself. The finding reveals how cells fine-tune their DNA-packing machinery. Precise levels matter, since these proteins govern which genes stay silent.
plos-pone-0005189:
Cells that start out alike do not always end up alike, even when their genes are the same. Le and Cheng used a single-cell approach in PLOS ONE in 2009 to study that spread during fat cell formation. They worked with a standard lab cell line that can turn into fat-storing cells.

By profiling cells one by one, the pair traced the varied outcomes to causes that are not changes in the genes themselves. The work shows where the split in cell fates begins. That matters for stem cell work, where getting every cell to follow the same path is a core problem.
plos-pone-0005289:
Children with autism are often reported to react less to pain, a claim with real care implications. Theories tied that report to opioids, the body's own pain-relief chemicals. Tordjman and colleagues tested pain responses and blood beta-endorphin in children and teens with autism in PLOS ONE in 2009.

The study measured behavior and body responses to pain in a large group, alongside plasma levels of beta-endorphin. Comparing the measures tests whether the opioid theory holds. Solid data here matter, because assuming low pain sensitivity can lead to undertreated pain in autistic youth.
plos-pone-0005889:
Andrew Williams and co-authors profiled small RNAs in the airways of people with mild asthma in 2009, before and after steroid treatment. Asthma brings reversible airway narrowing and chronic inflammation, usually treated with inhaled corticosteroids. MicroRNAs, a newer class of gene regulators, had barely been mapped in asthmatic airways.

The team measured microRNA patterns in airway samples and how budesonide changed them. Distinct patterns could serve as markers of disease or of treatment response. Such markers might one day guide steroid dosing per patient. The study is an early atlas of these regulators in a common disease.
plos-pone-0005989:
Paying heed and remembering seem like two jobs, yet they may share one crew. Bruno van Swinderen, Amber McCartney, Sarah Kauffman and colleagues tested that link in fruit flies in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper uses Drosophila, whose brain is small enough to study whole, and mutants known to fail at smell and sight memory tasks.

Flies that cannot form memories also show flaws in visual attention, the team reports. The overlap suggests both jobs draw on shared systems in the fly brain. A shared-system result in so simple an animal hints the link runs deep in evolution, and it gives brain science a lean model for studying two core skills at once.
plos-pone-0006089:
Yeast cells keep their shape by organizing actin, the protein cable that braces them. Shuguang Guo, Xiaoyun Shen, Gonghong Yan and colleagues mapped a feedback loop behind that order in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper studies Rho1, a switch protein that controls actin layout and cell wall growth in baker's yeast, and the stress pathway that answers when the wall is harmed.

A MAP kinase-dependent feedback mechanism governs Rho1 and where actin gathers, the title reports. Feedback keeps a stressed cell from overcorrecting as it patches its wall. The loop is a neat case of a cell steering itself, and its parts have cousins in human cells, which makes yeast a useful first draft.
plos-pone-0006189:
Insulin does more than control blood sugar; it also tells the body to build fat cells. Hui Zhang and colleagues traced the route of that order in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. Insulin and its signal protein Akt were known to be required for fat formation, but which branch below them mattered most was unclear.

The team shows the signal runs through Akt, then TSC2, then a growth switch called mTORC1. Blocking that chain blocks the making of new fat cells. A clear route map helps researchers study obesity and diabetes with sharper tools. It also flags points where future drugs might adjust fat storage.
plos-pone-0006689:
Youhei Egami and Nobukazu Araki filmed a protein at work inside living cells for PLOS ONE in 2009. The protein is Rab21, part of the Rab family that manages membrane traffic. Its role in macropinocytosis was unclear. Macropinocytosis is how cells gulp large sips of surrounding fluid. Macrophages use it while sampling their environment and hunting invaders.

The researchers watched Rab21 in live RAW264 macrophages stimulated with a growth factor. Fluorescent tags let them follow the protein in space and time. They recorded dynamic changes in where Rab21 gathered during the gulping process. Those movements place Rab21 at specific steps of membrane traffic. The findings clarify how macrophages organize this form of uptake.
plos-pone-0006789:
Dennis J. Bua and colleagues built a platform for mapping how proteins read histone marks in PLOS ONE in 2009. Histones carry many chemical modifications after they are made. Protein domains act as readers of those marks. Readers translate marks into nuclear and epigenetic programs. Mutations in reader domains appear in disease.

Their epigenome microarray platform surveys readers across the proteome. It dissects chromatin-signaling networks in a systematic way. A proteome-wide view shows which domains bind which marks. That map helps explain how epigenetic information is interpreted. It can also reveal drug targets among misbehaving reader proteins.
plos-pone-0006889:
Paul Gratraud and his team took the measure of a fat-making enzyme in the malaria germ in PLOS ONE in 2009. The germ Plasmodium falciparum swells the fat in the red blood cells it haunts. One fat, oleic acid, swells most. How the germ gets that fat was a riddle. The enzyme here is stearoyl-CoA desaturase, which makes just such fats.

The team set out the enzyme's traits in full. They also weighed it as a drug aim. A germ that must make its own fat has a weak spot in the path. Jam that path, and the germ may starve in its blood cell home. The full traits are step one toward drugs that jam it.
plos-pone-0006989:
Xuqing Zhang, Maria Eugenia Rodríguez, and Eric Harvill studied whooping cough relatives in PLOS ONE in 2009. Bordetella parapertussis causes a milder form of whooping cough. Vaccines built only from B. pertussis antigens give it little protection, if any. Why the vaccine's antibodies fail against the relative was the puzzle.

The team traced the failure to a surface feature called the O antigen. That shield blocks cross-reactive antibodies from binding and doing their work. The finding explains a real gap in vaccine coverage. Future whooping cough vaccines may need parts from both species.
plos-pone-0007089:
Saloua Toujani, Philippe Dessen, Nathalie Ithzar, and colleagues scanned Burkitt's lymphoma genomes in PLOS ONE in 2009. Extra chromosome changes are common in this fast-growing lymphoma. They shape how the disease progresses and how patients fare. The genes involved in those changes were still elusive.

The team ran a whole-genome array analysis at high resolution. They cross-checked the results with karyotypes and targeted FISH tests. Their catalogue sharpens the list of altered regions in these tumors. Each narrowed region is a hunting ground for the genes that push this lymphoma forward.
plos-pone-0007189:
Fernando Siso-Nadal, Jeffrey J. Fox, Stéphane A. Laporte, and colleagues modeled cell signaling in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Cells turn many outside stimuli into just a few inside messengers. Two of those messengers, calcium and cAMP, can rise and fall in repeating waves called oscillations.

The authors study how talk between signaling pathways can produce steady, robust oscillations. Their model links calcium and cAMP rhythms instead of treating each alone. Cell biologists can use the work to understand how cells encode decisions in timed pulses rather than steady signals.
plos-pone-0007289:
Camille Lebarbenchon, Frédéric Albespy, Anne-Laure Brochet, and colleagues tracked avian influenza spread by ducks in Europe in 2009. Highly pathogenic H5N1 viruses had recently spread widely. Dispersal of avian influenza viruses became a growing research focus, because bird movements can carry viruses across continents in weeks.

The authors study the common teal, a small migratory duck. They relate local and migratory movements to virus spread. Their PLOS ONE work examines how teal could move avian influenza viruses within Europe. Such host movement data help officials anticipate where outbreaks may appear next.
openalex-w2049309389: Dementia before 65 is rare, real, and underdiagnosed. Vieira and colleagues' 2013 review surveyed the epidemiology of early-onset dementia. The literature review mapped prevalence and causes of presenile dementia across studies — a public health blind spot.
openalex-w2069283089: Dengue's mosquito dances to climate and human rhythms. Stewart Ibarra and colleagues' 2013 study examined dengue vector dynamics in Ecuador, influenced by climate and social factors. The work guided targeted control of Aedes aegypti where it matters most.
openalex-w2123160589: Muons must be caught cleanly — ATLAS tuned its net. The ATLAS team's 2014 paper measured muon catching in 2011–2012 collisions. The work pinned efficiency and momentum scale — the detector, tuned and ready for physics at last, fully and now.
plos-pone-0006289:
Bacteria that live in slime layers called biofilms resist antibiotics and immune attack. Tim Conibear, Samuel Collins, and Jeremy Webb asked what mutation does inside growing biofilms of Pseudomonas aeruginosa, in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Biofilms grow into dense three-dimensional microcolonies of hard-to-kill cells.

The study examines how genetic change contributes to biofilm development itself. Mutation may help populations diversify and adapt within the film. Understanding that process bears on chronic infections where biofilms persist for years. It may suggest ways to break biofilms by targeting their evolution.
plos-pone-0009689:
Bile acids help digest fats, but in newborns with liver trouble they can reach the heart. Siti Sheikh Abdul Kadir and colleagues studied that danger in newborn rat heart cells in 2010. Their PLOS ONE report traced how bile acids disturb the heartbeat.

The disturbed rhythm ran through muscarinic M2 receptors, docking sites on the heart cells. Blocking that pathway changed the effect, which pinned down the route involved. The finding links a digestive chemical to heart rhythm problems in the very young. It may help doctors watch infants whose livers cannot clear bile well.
openalex-w2793318989: In the weakly electric fish Gymnotus omarorum, dominants are fiercely aggressive and subordinates submit in precise sequences of movement and electric signals. This 2018 Frontiers in Behavioral Neuroscience paper shows the hormone vasotocin modulates this hierarchy differently by status. The fish offer a clean window into the neurochemistry of dominance.
openalex-w2809443489: Connectivity is a core concept for understanding complex systems — used differently in every discipline. This 2018 Applied Network Science paper takes a multi-disciplinary perspective, comparing how fields conceptualize and operationalize connectivity. The synthesis looks for common ground beneath disciplinary boundaries.
openalex-w2898372989: Respiratory viruses can reach the brain — and the neurological aftermath can be severe. This 2018 Frontiers in Cellular Neuroscience paper reviews how infections like measles and herpes viruses cause lasting neurologic sequelae. The review connects familiar respiratory pathogens to their underappreciated brain damage.
openalex-w2952488689: Genomic prediction in cattle breeding leans on single-step GBLUP — but its marker effects lacked formal hypothesis testing. Qitao Tan and eight co-authors tackle a safety problem that appears when language models are shrunk for use. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that public models are safety-aligned in pretraining. Fine-tuning for a real task then often erodes that alignment and adds fresh safety risks.

Older defenses rebuild safety during fine-tuning or fix the model afterward with training-derived priors. Both routes tie safety recovery to training and carry high compute cost. The proposed method, Q-realign, attaches realignment to quantization, the step that compresses a model for deployment. The goal is safe and efficient deployment without a complex extra workflow.
arxiv-2601-08489:
Tony Cristofano studies how to remove refusal behavior from language models without harming their skill. His 2026 arXiv paper notes that safety-aligned models systematically refuse harmful requests. Recent work shows refusal can be steered through low-dimensional activation changes.

Directly ablating the refusal vector often causes collateral damage, though. The vector is computed from contrastive harmful and harmless prompts, and cutting it can drift general behavior. Cristofano proposes concept-guided spectral cleaning to separate safety from intelligence more cleanly. The topic is sensitive: the same methods that audit alignment could weaken it. Careful analysis helps defenders see how fragile refusal training may be.
arxiv-2601-06689:

arxiv-2601-07989:
Abdelaziz Bounhar, Mireille Sarkiss, and Michèle Wigger find the exact error exponent for distributed detection under tight communication limits. A sensor must report to a decision center over a discrete memoryless channel. Three stringent constraints are studied. In one, channel uses grow slower than the number of observations. In another, channel uses equal the observation count with further restrictions. Their 2026 preprint identifies the Stein exponent in these regimes.

The Stein exponent governs how fast detection errors vanish with more data. Distributed detection underlies sensor networks for environment, health, and security monitoring. Tight channel limits reflect real radios with little power or bandwidth. Exact exponents tell engineers the best any system can do. The paper serves information theorists and sensor network designers. It completes a theoretical picture for constrained detection.

arxiv-2601-08589: Kiumars Aryana, D. Bailey, Solomon Woods, and Adam Fleisher wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on a small tool that splits light into fine bands. arxiv-2601-08789:

At those turns, the algebras gain rich new traits. They are tied to a smooth group and to a surface with holes and one edge.

The team tracks how the algebras can act on state spaces at those turns. Such acts are called representations. They can code knot and link traits, and states in quantum shape work.
