arxiv-2601-09189:
Juan Carlos Agurto and three co-authors give a lab test that lets a class see two famed guards of plasma physics. In a field trap, a charged bit keeps two counts near fixed as it loops. One is its magnetic moment. The next is a length sum along its path. Books oft treat both as pure math, since a live show is hard to stage.

The team uses a school e/m kit, set as a field bottle trap. Pupils can watch the bit path and sum both guards from real marks. The sums hold, as the books claim. A reader who teaches physics gets a hands on show for a pair of laws that can feel far from real.
arxiv-2601-09289:
Takashi Horiyama and six co-authors map the hard grade of a card game called Swish. In the game, cards hold hoops and balls in set spots. Lay cards on each so hoops meet balls in all spots, and you have a swish. Past work by Dailly and team set grades for a broad form of the game by signs per card.

With one sign per card, the game can be solved fast. With three or more, it is in the hard class where no fast full solve is thought to live. This team fills gaps in that map, case by case. A reader in play math gets a sharp line for a fun game: where fun stays fair, and where it turns hard.
arxiv-2601-09489:
Peyman Afshani and five co-authors tackle a counting problem over streams of visits. Their 2026 arXiv paper asks, given many users moving among many regions, how many users stayed long in total. Each user's time is spread across regions, and only the summed time counts.

Answering exactly would need tracking every user in full detail. The authors seek fast methods, drawing on data structures, sketching, and sampling. They also prove lower bounds that mark what no method can beat. Problems like this arise in location analytics, where firms must count loyal visitors without storing raw trails.
arxiv-2601-10189:
Jonathan Vieth, Annika Eichler, and Arne Speerforck build smart controls for heat and cool rigs. Such rigs must use less power to cut carbon. A control that plans ahead can do that. But it needs a true model of the rig. Those models are oft built in blocks of fixed size.

The team made a frame that builds the control on its own. It sets the time steps and the block cuts. It then forms a plan ahead control from the model. The aim is less hand work and a better plan. That helps heat rigs run clean and cheap.
arxiv-2601-10789:
Z. Kaczmarek, A. Halasi-Kun, P. McGill, S. E. Perkins, and W. A. Dawson look for isolated neutron stars with the Roman Space Telescope. Neutron stars alone in space are hard to detect and study. Yet they hold clues about how stars live and explode. Roman, set to launch in 2026, opens a new channel: astrometric microlensing.

In microlensing, a passing star's gravity bends light and shifts a background star's apparent place. An isolated neutron star would leave such a shift with no visible lens. The authors assess what Roman can learn from these events. The work plans a census of dead stars that no telescope can see directly.
arxiv-2601-11089:
Suhan Guo, Jiahong Deng, and Furao Shen present MiCA, a causal adapter for epidemic forecasting that uses mobility data. Forecasting infectious disease guides public health planning and response. Human mobility drives how epidemics spread across space. But mobility data are noisy and indirect, and case series are short and coarsely reported. Both flaws fight the forecaster.

MiCA, short for Mobility-Informed Causal Adapter, is built to stay lightweight. It aims to fold mobility into case forecasts without letting noise run the show. A causal angle helps separate true spread signals from coincidence. The work serves health agencies that need timely local forecasts from thin, messy data during an outbreak's early weeks.
arxiv-2601-10989:
Yancy L. Shirley, Jeffrey G. Mangum, Desika Narayanan, and James Di Francesco explain how thermal dust emission reveals the traits of dusty objects in space. Dust grains soak up short-wave light and reradiate it at long waves. They shift photon energy across the spectrum. Thermal glow from dust between the stars was first seen sixty years ago, in 1965.

The authors set out how to turn that emission into physical traits: mass, heat, and density. Such readings support studies of star forming clouds and galaxies. Getting them right depends on grain properties and on careful modeling. The paper serves the teams who use telescopes like ALMA to weigh the cold universe and gauge its cold.
arxiv-2601-11789:
Shenyang Deng, Boyao Liao, Zhuoli Ouyang, Tianyu Pang, Minhak Song, and Yaoqing Yang study a quirk in how gradient descent trains models. When the loss surface is steep in a few ways and flat in the rest, steps can align in odd ways. They call this the suspicious alignment effect.

In the first phase of training, the step's link to the steep part tends to drop. They give a fine step size rule that tracks this effect. Such rules help set step size with care. Good step picks can speed training and dodge poor end points in hard loss fields.
arxiv-2601-12189:
Xiangdong Ji, Yizhuang Liu, and Yushan Su expand Euclidean correlators at long distance for lattice parton work. Such correlators, with Wilson links, are used in large-momentum theory to compute parton physics from lattice QCD. Confinement makes them decay fast at large gaps.

That decay rules how well Fourier transforms can be done with low error. Their asymptotic expansion tracks the decay in a set form. Better long-distance control cuts errors in parton densities from lattice data. Those densities feed collider predictions.  Decay forms set error bars for parton work.  Such control is key for momentum space work.
arxiv-2601-11289:
Jung-Ho Kim and Alex Arenas study sync in power grids in this preprint. Their 2026 focus is on grids with more small generators. Clean energy growth adds many inverter-based sources to the grid. Each new unit is small next to an old power plant.

Sync of frequency is what keeps a grid stable and whole. A common guess says spread-out power should help sync. More small units would smooth the spread of node inputs. Less spread would mean less coupling is needed to lock in. The title states the team's twist on that guess. Spread can in fact hinder sync, through more than one phase shift. The result warns grid planners to test, not just trust the guess.
arxiv-2601-11489:
Trygve Poppe Oldervoll models infinity-categories with semi-simplicial spaces. His 2026 preprint studies quasi-unital inner Kan spaces. Infinity-categories are a vast upgrade of category theory. Models for them must capture maps at all levels at once.

His spaces meet two conditions for the model to work. First, inner horns fill up to homotopy in the space. Second, units exist in a weak sense through the structure. Quasi-unitality can be stated in more than one way. The literature holds three natural forms of the condition. Oldervoll compares those forms and their links to each other. The result backs a leaner model of higher categories.
arxiv-2601-13089:
Maryam Shooshtari, for the CMS team, re-reads data on a rare crash out come with four top quarks. Top quarks are the heaviest known bits. Making four at once is rare and hard to spot. The new read uses the full Run 2 data set from the CMS detector.

That data set holds 138 inverse femtobarns of proton crash data. The team uses it to test ideas that reach past the Standard Model. Four top events give a clean place to hunt for new forces or new bits that couple to top quarks. The paper shows how an old data set can be mined a fresh way to set tight bounds on new physics.
arxiv-2601-13189:
Paolo Andreetto, Massimo Casarsa, and a large team set out a detector plan for a muon collider at huge energy. Muons are heavy kin of electrons. A muon and anti muon crash at 10 TeV would open a new realm for tests of matter. The full gain of such a plant rests on one thing, though.

The detector must cope with vast noise made by the machine itself. Their plan is called MUSIC. It is a muon system built for what they call the fun crashes, the rare ones that count. The paper gives how MUSIC would fare at that energy. For collider planners, the work shows one path to a detector that can live with the noise and still catch new physics.
arxiv-2601-13289:
Ruhul Amin Khalil and co-authors send sense, not raw bits, through sea nets to save scarce room. The Internet of Underwater Things links sensors for sea watch, reef health, and deep search. Sea links are harsh, though. Room is thin, lag is high, and power is tight. Raw data first nets waste all three.

Sense first links send what a read means, in brief form, in place of the full raw read. The team sets out how such links can work in sea nets. They weigh gains in room and power next to the risk of lost detail. For sea teams, the trade may be the price of nets that last.
arxiv-2601-13389:
Zhaohui Liang, Chengyuan Ma, Keke Long, Hang Zhou, and Xiaopeng Li stress test eco driving plans at signal lights. Eco driving eases speed to cut fuel use and fumes, most of all near lights where stops waste the most. Past tests of such plans used neat sims or tight lab terms.

Those neat terms can flatter a plan. Real roads add mixed traffic, late lights, and driver quirks. The team asks how strong and how springy such plans stay when terms turn rough. A plan that only wins in a neat sim is of thin worth. Their checks aim to sort plans that hold up on real streets.
arxiv-2601-13489:
Shuyuan You and co-authors ask if deep auction tools can trust their own regret scores. New tools such as RegretNet learn near best multi item auctions by nets. They loose the rule that no bidder gains by a lie, then score that breach by ex post regret. A low score is meant to show near sound acts.

Yet the true score is hard to sum in full. Tools use gradient search, whose out come bends with knob picks. So a low read score may hide a high true score. The team seeks a firm bridge from read score to true score. For auction teams, a regret score that can be trusted is the base of the whole route.
arxiv-2601-12489:
M. L. Nekrasov studies parton distribution functions at small values of the momentum fraction x. These functions say how the momentum of a fast proton is shared among its parts. At small x, the proton looks dense with low momentum partons. That regime is hard, since it falls in a non perturbative zone where standard tools fail.

Nekrasov uses an upgraded parton model with both splitting and fusion of partons. For moderately small x, he finds a power law form for the parton density. The exponent of that law ties to the log of the splitting probability. Once fusion is added, the equation for the density turns nonlinear. That shift captures how partons merge when the crowd gets dense.
arxiv-2601-13589:
HyeYoung Lee presents a team of AI agents that makes media in real time in 2026. The system listens to sound and reads the mood in a voice. It then builds a reply that fits that mood. Most past work on speech mood stops at naming the mood with care. Lee shifts the focus to what the system says back.

A chain of agents, each with its own job, shapes the reply step by step. Safety checks run as the content is made, not after the fact. The replies aim to be safe, fit the user's age, and stay under clear control. The design suits live tools where a bad reply can do harm fast.
arxiv-2601-13689:
Vahid Pooryousef and co-authors build an XR tool to rebuild crime scenes in motion in 2026. Police have grown keen on 3D models for virtual scene work. Models let teams study a scene off-site, with no cost or risk of tainting real proof. Past tools show where things stood, in static form.

Their tool, Criminator, animates the scene so events unfold in time. Checking the order of events is key to solving many cases. A dynamic scene lets teams test if a claimed sequence could have happened. The tool aims for rapid setup that busy teams can use.
arxiv-2601-13889:
Wenge Xu and co-authors study car-to-pedestrian signals for deaf and hard-of-hearing people in 2026. External human-machine interfaces, or eHMIs, let automated vehicles signal intent to people on foot. No past work had focused on deaf and hard-of-hearing users. The team ran focus groups to fill that gap.

Six deaf or hard-of-hearing people took part, plus six key stakeholders. Stakeholders included researchers, assistive technologists, and automotive interface designers. They compared proposed visual and auditory eHMIs and drew out design requirements. Inclusive signals are a must if driverless cars are to be safe for all. Their list of needs can guide car firms as they draw up new dash and door signs. It puts deaf and hard-of-hearing users at the start of design, not at the end.
arxiv-2601-14089:
Zhenxu Zhao, Ji Wang, and Weiyao Lan build safe control from data for a class of systems in 2026. The systems are linear with a known strict-feedback structure. Most plant parameters, external disturbances, and input delay are unknown. Koopman operator theory lets them learn dynamics from measured data.

They use Krylov dynamic mode decomposition to extract the dynamics. That enables reconstruction of the system and disturbance matrices. Their frame targets safe output regulation despite the unknowns and delay. Data-driven safety suits plants that are hard to model but easy to observe.
arxiv-2601-14389:
Can Kilic, Sanjay Mathai, and Taewook Youn study particles called Loryons in this 2026 paper. Loryons are particles beyond the Standard Model. They get a significant fraction of their mass from electroweak symmetry breaking, the event that gave known particles their masses. That trait makes them a marked target for collider searches.

The team places Loryons inside a two Higgs doublet model. That model adds a second Higgs field to the standard one. Inside that frame, they work out the constraints on Loryons. Readers get bounds on where such particles could still hide, given what experiments have and have not seen.
arxiv-2601-14789:
Toshihiro Yada, Nobuyuki Yoshioka, and Takahiro Sagawa test thermal behavior in quantum systems in this 2026 paper. Understanding the thermal behavior of quantum many-body pure states is one of the most fundamental issues in quantum thermodynamics. It is widely known that typical pure states yield vanishing work, just as thermal states do. That holds when one restricts to local operations that cannot access correlations among subsystems.

The team tests equivalence to thermal states via extractable work under LOCC. LOCC means local operations plus classical communication between the parts. Work that can be extracted is a concrete thermometer for state likeness. Readers get a sharp test of when a single pure state truly acts like a hot ensemble.
arxiv-2601-15489:
Archana Maji builds de Sitter space inside string theory in a 2026 arXiv paper. De Sitter space is the geometry of a universe with steady expansion. String theory has long struggled to host it as a vacuum state. No-go theorems block many such attempts. Maji takes a different route. She constructs four-dimensional de Sitter space as an excited state instead.

An excited state is not the lowest-energy vacuum. That shift lets the framework sidestep vacuum-based bans, she argues. The construction spans several string theories. They include type IIB and both heterotic forms, based on SO(32) and E8 times E8. The paper is a computational companion, per its title. For cosmology, the stakes are plain. Our own universe looks de Sitter-like, so string theory needs a home for it.
arxiv-2601-15589:
Xuan Liao, Zhenkang Peng, and Ying Rong study ordering for goods that spoil in a 2026 arXiv paper. Managing perishable products is a basic challenge in inventory work. Poor ordering leads to stockouts or heavy waste. Their system adds random lead times to the mix. Neither the demand process nor the lead time distribution is known to the decision maker. Both must be learned while ordering.

The title adds two ingredients: deep learning and human knowledge. Pure learning can stumble when data are thin or patterns shift. Human expertise holds practical rules that data alone may miss. Blending the two aims for orders that waste less and miss less. Grocery and pharmacy supply chains face this problem daily. Better policies cut cost and keep shelves filled with fresh stock.
arxiv-2601-15089:
Zhuchao Ji, Jiarui Song, and Junyi Xie prove a bound on torsion points of abelian schemes. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with families of abelian varieties set over a smooth curve. Torsion points are points that return to the identity after a fixed number of steps.

Their route is geometric. For a non-isotrivial family, they show the genus of generic multi-sections with small heights grows without bound. From that growth they give a fresh proof of a known result. The count of prime-power torsion points stays uniform across the fibers of the family.
arxiv-2601-15289:
A. Ahmed, W. H. Elsanhoury, and co-authors trace the Milky Way's disk through three old star clusters. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies Berkeley 17, 18, and 39, clusters of intermediate to old age. They use precise position and brightness data from the Gaia mission's third data release.

Cluster membership is the first problem, since field stars crowd the same view. The team sorts members by a probabilistic study of proper motions. The clean samples hold hundreds of stars in each cluster. Those samples let them read the clusters' traits and their place in the galactic disk.
arxiv-2601-16089:
Sylvain Procope-Mamert and three coauthors set out a fresh way to pick paths in grain filters. Their 2026 preprint deals with filters that track a state from a stream of views. Good paths, called proposals, guide which states the filter tests. Past online ways build paths by work from the end back. That needs the full data set in hand.

The new way works forth, step by step, as data comes in. It uses views yet to come to hone the paths so far. Forth work fits live use, where the end is not yet known. The team tests if forth paths can match back built ones. The work aims at fast live state tracking.
arxiv-2601-16189:
Xiaotian Yang and coauthors test if a grid code can make Bell tests work with plain reads. Their 2026 preprint deals with Bell tests that use wave reads. Wave reads in such tests face tight caps on what they can show. The team asks if GKP code can lift those caps. GKP code stores a bit in a wave like state on a grid.

Each side reads the wave and turns the result to bits. The team models that full chain with real gear terms. Strong Bell breaks in that chain would prove the code path works. Such breaks show non local links in a firm test. The work links code choice to test strength.
arxiv-2601-16389:
Itsuki Shimamura and coauthors make a tri spin chain in a verdazyl based nickel mix. Their 2026 preprint reports a new made mix in the lab. Nickel ions and verdazyl free parts form the chain. The chain holds spin half and spin one units in a row. Those units sit in a tri form that loops down the chain.

Math sums of the core states show strong anti line pulls. Anti pulls mean near spins point in flip ways. A clean tri chain lets teams test spin maths in real stuff. Past tri chains were hard to make in pure form. The work gives a new test bed for spin chains.
arxiv-2601-17189:
Sabrina Mokhtari, Sara Kodeiri, Shubhankar Mohapatra, Florian Tramèr, and Gautam Kamath reset the test base for private image AI. Private learn keeps train facts hid as it learns. Image sort is its most-checked task by far. Their 2026 preprint says old test sets skew the grades. They set out a fuller set in its place. It spans work with and sans extra data.

Convex tasks join the set for clean base reads. Unlike data sets test how broad a tool's skill is. Fair sets stop teams from games with pick-of-task. Private AI grades then mean more for real use.
arxiv-2601-17589:
Thomas Sandholm and three co-authors present SpaceCoMP for computing in orbit. Thousands of satellites image Earth each day. Most of that data never reaches the ground. Downlink bandwidth cannot keep up. The team proposes processing in the low Earth orbit zone itself. SpaceCoMP is a MapReduce-inspired model for satellite mesh networks.

Compute near the data cuts what must be sent down. Satellites can filter, merge, and summarize images in orbit. Only the useful results take the narrow link home. That shift could unlock data now lost. Earth watch, disaster maps, and climate work all gain. The model fits a space era of dense satellite fleets.
arxiv-2601-17989:
Justin Downes studies networks that grow by attachment but also lose their links. His 2026 preprint deals with synthetic growing networks. Classic models add one node at a time. Each new node brings a fixed count of edges, and those edges then stay frozen for all later steps. Real networks rarely behave that way. Links fade, lapse, and get cut as the network ages.

Downes lets decay act on the evolving network alongside attachment. The mix changes the degree patterns that growth alone would give. Many real systems, from friendships to citations, show both forces at once. A model with decay can match such systems more closely. The work refines a basic tool for network science.
arxiv-2601-18089:
Venmugil Elango and co-authors ask how close today's mixture-of-experts models are to the best possible use of compute. Their 2026 preprint studies MoE designs, now central to top open and closed language models. An MoE routes each token to a few expert parts, so cost per token stays low. Yet no one knew how much accuracy each unit of compute or each parameter could in principle buy. The authors frame that gap as accuracy per FLOP and per parameter.

Their study, named LatentMoE in the title, probes where the waste sits. Knowing the ceiling helps designers spend on the right parts. At the scale of modern training runs, even small gains save vast sums.
arxiv-2601-18189:
Rui Wu and Yongjun Li give causal discovery a method that lands exactly on a graph in finite time. Their 2026 preprint builds on continuous optimization, the approach made famous by NOTEARS. Such methods usually promise only that they approach a fixed point as steps go on forever. In practice they return dense weighted matrices. Users then cut weak edges by a threshold picked by hand, which makes the found graph shaky.

The authors use smoothed proximal gradients to fix that. Their method recovers an exact skeleton, and it does so in finite time. The result is smooth, sparse, and stable, as their title says. Cleaner causal graphs matter wherever cause, not just correlation, drives a choice.
arxiv-2601-18289:
Jialong Li and co-authors present Quest2ROS2, an open-source frame for two-handed robot teleoperation in virtual reality. Their 2026 preprint builds on the earlier Quest2ROS. Robot data collection needs to scale, and human-guided robots are a main source of training data. The old frame's workspace limits held that back. Quest2ROS2 uses relative motion control: the robot's move is computed from changes in the VR controller's pose. That makes control intuitive and free of the user's exact stance.

Pose-independent control lets operators work from any position. Two hands at once suit tasks from assembly to care. An open frame lets labs share the same data tools. The work feeds the data engine behind robot learning.
arxiv-2601-19589: A short note in differential geometry takes up a question about graph Laplace operators. The operator studied is the continuous intrinsic version, built with a Gaussian kernel on a compact curved surface with no boundary. The note shows that this operator alone determines two things. One is the surface's metric, which fixes all distances. The other is the density of the sampling points, as long as that density stays positive. In short, the operator remembers the shape it came from.
arxiv-2601-19989:
Damien Korber and colleagues measure the chemistry of faint galaxies seen as they were in the early universe. The GLIMPSE-D survey uses gravitational lensing, where massive clusters magnify distant galaxies. That boost reveals galaxies far fainter than telescopes could normally study, at redshifts between six and nine. The team measures an emission-line ratio in several dozen of them.

That ratio tracks the abundance of oxygen, a proxy for overall metallicity. Calibrated relations turn the ratio into abundances galaxy by galaxy. The sample reaches very low luminosities, testing how metals declined among the faintest systems. The authors also draw out what the trend means for counting such galaxies by their line emission. Early chemical enrichment is a key chapter of cosmic history.
arxiv-2601-20089:
Qasim Javed, Harrison Tuckman, and Eric Neuscamman extend a quantum chemistry method to doubly excited states. Coupled cluster theory is a workhorse for computing molecular energies. The Aufbau suppressed variant tames its cost and instability for hard cases. Doubly excited states, where two electrons jump at once, are important for photochemistry but hard to reach.

The authors derive, implement, and test an initialization strategy for these states. It lets the starting wavefunction match the largest configurations of a doubly excited reference. The method keeps the same asymptotic cost as standard singles and doubles theory. Cheaper access to doubly excited states aids the study of light-driven chemistry. The work generalises a promising formalism rather than bolting on a fix.
arxiv-2601-20289:
Davesh Maulik, Junliang Shen, and Qizheng Yin study the Orlov conjecture for hyper-Kähler varieties, a deep question in algebraic geometry. Their route uses Fourier transforms built from projectively hyperholomorphic bundles, following Markman's work, on products of these varieties. They focus on varieties of the type built from K3 surfaces.

As applications, they prove that derived equivalent varieties of this type have isomorphic homological motives that preserve the cup product. Motives are meant to capture the shared shape beneath different cohomology theories. Results of this kind test how much of a variety's geometry is fixed by its derived category.
arxiv-2601-20489:
B. Hagedorn and four colleagues map a massive dusty outflow in a nearby merging galaxy and find it shows no sign of slowing across kiloparsec scales. The galaxy is an ultraluminous infrared system, bright from intense star formation in a merger. They combine ALMA observations of cold molecular gas with optical data that trace ionized and neutral gas and dust.

Tracking the outflow in several phases at once shows how the wind carries mass and energy out of the galaxy. An outflow that keeps its speed far out can starve future star formation, shaping how the merged galaxy evolves.
arxiv-2601-20589:
Lucas Kook and Søren Wengel Mogensen study exact learning of graphs through integer programming. Learning the dependence structure among variables is central across medical, natural, and social science. These structures are naturally drawn as graphs, and inferring them from data is called graph learning, or causal discovery when the graph is read causally.

Exact methods guarantee the best-fitting graph under a stated score, unlike greedy searches. Integer programming gives a route to that exactness. Guarantees matter when a learned graph will guide experiments or policy, and an approximate graph could mislead both.
arxiv-2601-18889:
R. Noah Padgett builds a way to test if a lone quiz item acts in a fair way across lands and groups. Such a test is called a check for item bias. It asks if folk with the same true skill, but from unlike groups, pass the item at the same rate. Past tests need more than one item to work. With a lone item there is no mate item to set the skill scale, and no trait to lean on as a stand-in.

Padgett adds a fine for wild swings to a kind of ordered score model that can take spread in its counts. The fine keeps the model from chase of noise in thin groups. A sound lone-item test could serve short polls and health checks that have just one item per trait. Those are in wide use across lands, so fair checks count.
arxiv-2601-18789:
Agnijo Banerjee and Lawrence Hollom study a fair-fill task in the maths of graphs. A graph is filled fair when each hue in a set shows the same count of times. Take a full graph whose points come in set blocks, filled fair with a set count of hues. The task asks if one can pick a sub-graph of a set form that spans all points and keeps the fair fill.

The form to span is set in the task, with a set count of points. The sub-graph must take each point once and hold the hue counts of the whole in its own links. A past scholar set the ask. The pair take it up and pin when the span can be found. Such asks tie the maths of fill to the maths of span. Both serve codes and plans.
arxiv-2601-18689:
Benjamin Kang, Yury Polyanskiy, and Anzo Teh study how to guess a trait of a hid fact from a set of noisy reads of like facts. Each read in the set springs from its own hid fact, and the hid facts all come from one shared pool. The task is to guess a set trait of one hid fact, given its read. The guess can lean on all reads, since the pool is shared. That lean is the heart of the school named for Bayes in its field form.

The pair of authors and their mate look at two kinds of read: counts that jump by whole steps, and reads that hum with a bell-shaped hiss. For both, they ask how well a guess can do. Sharp bounds on that ask guide tools in health, in surveys, and in code that learns from crowds.
arxiv-2601-21289:
Akash Pandey, Payal Mohapatra, Wei Chen, Qi Zhu, and Sinan Keten make time series models easier to explain. Knowing which stretch of a signal drove a prediction is key to trusting the model. Popular explanation tools lean on gradients or single-point scores, and both can mislead.

Their method, TimeSliver, splits the model into a symbolic part and a linear part. That split lets each time segment get a clear share of the credit. It also respects the order of events, which point-by-point tools ignore. Clearer credit helps users in fields like health and energy judge when a forecast deserves trust.
arxiv-2601-21689:
Agnibha De Sarkar examines the glow around a middle-aged pulsar that may form a pulsar halo. Extended gamma-ray sources near such pulsars are read as halos, where electrons escape and scatter starlight up to high energies. The source studied is tied to a bright, radio-quiet pulsar.

Its halo status is still uncertain. The author studies its emission signatures to test the halo reading against rivals. Halos matter because they reveal how cosmic rays spread through the galaxy near their sources. Confirming or rejecting one sharpens the map of that spread.
arxiv-2601-22389:
Bruce Stephenson and Robin Macomber find that many fields, each on its own, built the same tools to spot tipping points. A tipping point here is a phase shift, where ties stretch far and small nudges have huge effects. Their 2026 preprint surveys six to nine fields across nine decades.

Again and again, scholars derived near-identical measures of how ties scale near the edge. Few knew of the match across fields. Naming the shared core can save each field from rework. It may also yield one strong, shared test for early warning signs. The survey spans physics to social science.
arxiv-2601-22489:
Mohammad Rowshan sets the terms a quantum code must meet to serve as a fountain of magic states. Magic states fuel the hard gates that make quantum machines more than classical ones. His 2026 preprint works with qLDPC codes, which promise steady rates and long reach with light checks.

No known family of this kind yet meets all four marks at once: steady rate, long reach, light checks, and native three-way gates. Rowshan lays out the structural terms that would allow it. Clear terms guide the search for such a family. A find would cut the cost of quantum computing a great deal.
arxiv-2601-22689:
Stina Klein and a team test whether helper robots and fair task splits cut the stigma faced by workers with disabilities. Robots can ease physical strain at work. Their 2026 preprint notes that the social side is less clear: visible help could raise stigma, or lower it.

The team study how co-workers judge assisted staff under varied task assignments. Reasonable splits — fair shares for all — seem to shape that judgment. The results can guide firms that add robots to mixed teams. Inclusion, not just output, is the measure here. The work keeps dignity in the frame.
arxiv-2601-21789:
Adia Lumadjeng, Ilker Birbil, and Erman Acar want classifiers that can explain themselves in plain mathematics. Many accurate models are black boxes, which is a problem where decisions need justification. Their 2026 preprint introduces ECSEL, a method that learns formal expressions built from signomial equations.

A signomial is a sum of terms, each a product of variables raised to powers. The authors note that many symbolic regression benchmarks hide exactly this kind of compact structure. ECSEL builds a closed-form expression that serves as both the classifier and its own explanation. A model you can read as an equation can be audited, debated, and trusted in a way that a weight matrix cannot.
arxiv-2601-21889:
J. Lamprecht and co-authors dissect the crowded center of the early-type galaxy FCC 47. Many galaxy centers host nuclear star clusters, among the densest stellar systems known, and often a supermassive black hole sits beside them. How those black holes formed is largely lost to history.

Star clusters, by contrast, keep the marks of their past in their stars' ages and motions. Mergers, slow accretion, and internal dynamics all leave traces. The team's 2026 preprint decomposes the nuclear region into its orbital parts to read that history. Work like this uses nearby galaxy centers as fossils, reconstructing how the densest neighborhoods in the universe were assembled.
arxiv-2601-21989:
Edith Cohen, Elena Gribelyuk, Jelani Nelson, and Uri Stemmer study streaming algorithms that can forget. In the resettable streaming model, data arrive as a stream, and the value of each key can grow or be reset to zero. The model fits live resource monitoring that supports deletions, and machine unlearning.

The team's 2026 preprint develops adaptively robust methods for this model. Adaptive robustness is a strong demand. The algorithm must keep its guarantees even when future inputs react to its earlier outputs. That is much harder than handling a fixed stream. Guarantees like this matter for monitoring systems that adversaries, or simply responsive users, can probe and steer.
arxiv-2601-22189:
Han-Yu Lin, Li-Wei Chen, and Hung-Shin Lee clean up compressed video before the damage settles. Standard video codecs leave compression artifacts that degrade how footage looks. Heavy enhancement models can fix them, but they cost too much for routine use.

The team's 2026 preprint proposes SCENE, a lightweight preprocessing framework that is aware of meaning. It folds semantic embeddings from a vision-language model into an efficient convolutional network. The system spends its effort where viewers notice, protecting faces, text, and key objects while smoothing the rest. Smarter preprocessing could raise the quality of streaming and video calls without raising bitrates, a gain felt on every screen.
arxiv-2601-22089:
Ilaria Colazzo and Geoffrey Janssens link a puzzle law to a branch of algebra. The law is the pentagon law. It sets rules for how paired maps must agree, and it shows up in physics and in the theory of types. Its set-based forms use plain sets and swaps that can be run both ways.

The pair ask how these set forms tie to Hopf algebras. Such algebras act a bit like groups of traits, with rules to split and join them. They prove that the finite set forms match Hopf algebras with a good basis trait. They also stretch a known rank list to more fields. The work shows how a plain law on sets can breed rich new structure.
arxiv-2601-20689:
Xinyue Li and six co-authors work on how machines judge the quality of a picture. Their 2026 paper uses large models that can read both images and text. Such models can rate image quality well, the team notes. But training them for this job is costly. It also needs many scores from human raters.

The team argues that the true bottleneck is not how well the model sees flaws. The hard part is scale calibration: matching the model's scores to the human score scale. Their framework splits the job in two. One part handles perception, how the image looks. The other part handles calibration, how scores line up. By splitting the two, the method needs far fewer human labels. That makes quality checks cheaper to run.
arxiv-2601-20789:
Open-weight coding agents hold a promise that closed systems cannot match, and this 2026 paper says that promise is now practical. Such agents can be specialized to a private codebase. They can store repo-specific knowledge directly in their weights. Until now, the cost and complexity of training kept that edge out of reach. The paper presents SERA, short for Soft-Verified Efficient Repository Agents.

The work argues the cost barrier has fallen far enough to cross. Its agents are built for work inside real software repositories. That focus lets a model learn the quirks of one codebase deeply. For teams with private code, an open agent they can train themselves is a real option. The study marks a shift in who can own a specialized coding agent.
arxiv-2601-20889:
Maurice van Putten argues that cosmic expansion is set by a global rule, not by local dynamics. His 2026 paper offers a Machian view of cosmology. Mach's principle ties local physics to the whole universe. Van Putten frames expansion through phase normalization of the gravitational path integral. That normalization is fixed by causal horizon boundary conditions. Horizons mark the edge of what can ever be seen.

In this framing, the cosmological conformal factor is not a moving part. It is a global gauge variable, fixed by the Hamiltonian constraint. That makes the classic conformal-factor problem inapplicable, he argues. The paper is a theoretical proposal, not a data study. It invites cosmologists to rethink what drives the expansion. Readers get a compact statement of an unusual route to the standard picture.
arxiv-2601-21189:
Arther Tian and four co-authors design rewards for networks where strangers run AI inference for each other. Their 2026 paper concerns decentralized LLM inference networks. Such networks need lightweight mechanisms to reward high-quality outputs. Latency and cost vary widely across nodes. Proof of Quality offers scalable verification. Evaluator nodes are sampled to score candidate outputs. Their scores aggregate into a consensus signal that sets rewards.

The authors make that proof adaptive and robust, with cost awareness built in. Honest, fast, cheap providers should earn more. Gaming the scores should be hard. The design fits open networks that cannot rely on a central referee. As inference decentralizes, quality proofs become core infrastructure. The paper contributes a mechanism for that emerging market.
arxiv-2512-01389:
Haoyu Lei and co-authors build a fast decoder for error correction codes. Those codes guard digital messages from noise. New diffusion-based decoders are sharp but slow. They need many rounds of sampling to clean a message. That lag hurts low-delay uses.

Their model uses consistency flow to decode in one step. It keeps a transformer core for strength. One-step decoding cuts delay by a large margin. If accuracy holds, the method could serve in fast links like mobile and satellite systems where each delay counts. One-step decoding also cuts energy use per message, which counts for battery-powered links in phones, sensors, and small satellites.
arxiv-2512-01489:
Girardi and a large Euclid team give the first census of dusty, massive objects in the Perseus field. How stars formed long ago rests on far-off dusty galaxies. Those galaxies hide much of their light in dust. Euclid's sharp wide views can find them in bulk.

The team counts dusty and massive systems in early release data. They gauge their traits and how common they are. A firm census anchors claims about star birth at early times. It also shows what Euclid will add over its full survey of the sky.
arxiv-2512-01689:
A study extends the Klebanov theorem to a product group of reals and a two-element group. Klebanov's result links linear forms in independent random variables. It asks when distinct forms can share the same law. Such results sit in probability's core limit theory.

The extension moves the setting to variables on that product group. Linear forms are built the same way from shared inputs. Group structure changes what equality of laws forces. Results like this refine when sums of random parts must be Gaussian or near it. Group-valued variables arise in directional data and phase systems, so the extension speaks to applied probability as well as pure theory.
arxiv-2512-01089:
Peter Jansen, Samiah Hassan, and Pragnya Narasimha present CodeDistiller in a 2025 paper on scientific coding agents. Automated scientific discovery systems generate and run code-based experiments on their own. Their reach is limited by the code they can reliably produce from built-in knowledge alone.

Current systems either mutate a few hand-crafted examples or work purely from what the model already knows. CodeDistiller automatically generates code libraries for such agents, distilling dependable routines they can reuse. A good library would raise both the quality and reach of automated experiments, letting agents attempt studies that free-form code generation cannot sustain.
arxiv-2512-01189:
Chunzheng Zhu and six coauthors reconstruct speech gestures from brain signals in a 2025 paper. Decoding what the brain is doing has long challenged brain science. Most earlier work rebuilt images or language from brain activity, asking what a person saw or heard.

Their work instead reconstructs co-speech gestures, the hand and body movements that accompany speech a person perceives. The method, fMRI2GES, reads functional MRI signals and uses two matched decoding steps to turn them into gestures. Rebuilding perceived gestures extends brain decoding from words and pictures into body language, a new channel for brain-computer interfaces.
arxiv-2601-22889:
Yuxuan Lou and eight co-authors present DiffuSpeech, a speech model that thinks before it speaks. Most speech models answer at once, so an early error gets spoken and cannot be taken back. Their slogan is silent thought, spoken answer.

The model drafts internal text reasoning alongside the spoken reply, using a shared diffusion process. The silent draft can catch mistakes before they reach the listener's ear. Clearer, better-checked speech could improve voice assistants, tutors, and hands-free tools. The spoken reasoning stays internal, so listeners hear only the final answer while the model still gains the benefit of thinking first. That split mirrors how people rehearse an answer before speaking it aloud in a meeting.
arxiv-2601-23089:
Chandrashekhar B. Khare and Alexander Merkurjev classify which finite groups have a certain lifting property. The property concerns representations, structured descriptions of groups, taken modulo a prime. Lifting asks whether a description modulo a prime can be raised to one modulo the prime squared.

They settle the classification completely, for all finite groups and all primes. Such lifting questions sit inside number theory's study of symmetry and equations. A full classification tells researchers exactly where to expect obstructions, and where lifts always exist. Mod prime representations and their lifts to prime-squared precision are the objects the full classification organizes.
arxiv-2601-23189:
Markus Schmassmann and three co-authors improve computer models of sunspots. Existing models fail to match the observed magnetic field pattern in sunspots. The mismatch traces to an wrongly boosted sideways field at the model's upper boundary.

Using the MURaM radiative MHD code, they explore other boundary setups. The aim is to reproduce both the magnetic and dynamic behavior of real sunspots. Better sunspot models support forecasts of solar activity that affects Earth. The MURaM code includes radiative transfer, so the models track both magnetic structure and the energy the spots radiate. Matching the observed sideways field pattern is the specific failure the other boundaries are meant to repair.
arxiv-2512-00089:
Forecasting wildfires weeks or months ahead is difficult, yet fire managers need that lead time. Ioannis Prapas and five co-authors present TeleViT in a 2025 study, a vision transformer built for subseasonal to seasonal wildfire forecasts. Short-term fire forecasts lean on local weather, but long-range ones cannot.

Long-range patterns depend on teleconnections, the links between climate patterns in distant parts of the Earth. TeleViT is designed to account for those global patterns when it predicts fire risk. Better seasonal outlooks could help agencies plan fuel treatments and place crews and equipment before fire season peaks. Fire agencies already use seasonal outlooks, so even modest gains in skill have practical value.
arxiv-2512-00289:
Physics-based vehicle models are simplified on purpose, so they never match a real car exactly. Nguyen Ly and co-authors develop a data-driven framework for learning and correcting vehicle dynamics in 2025. The dynamics are non-autonomous, driven by time-dependent control inputs.

Learning predictive models directly from temporal snapshot data is challenging when controls keep changing the system's behavior. The framework aims to correct model-form uncertainty rather than discard the physics model entirely. More faithful vehicle models support safer self-driving tests, better simulators, and control systems that trust their own predictions. Correction, rather than replacement, keeps the physical knowledge already inside standard models. Snapshot data is what test tracks and fleets actually record.
arxiv-2512-00389:
Adversarial training and AI alignment can both be framed as games between two neural networks. Deep Patel and Emmanouil-Vasileios Vlatakis-Gkaragkounis study solving such neural min-max games in 2025, focusing on architecture, initialization, and dynamics. The desirable outcomes are von Neumann-Nash equilibria of the game.

These games usually have non-convex, non-concave objectives, yet simple gradient methods often converge in practice. That puzzle suggests hidden geometric structure in the problems. Understanding when and why training converges would make robust optimization and alignment methods more dependable across applications. Zero-sum framing fits adversarial training, where one network attacks and the other defends. Von Neumann's name on the equilibrium ties the work to classic game theory.
arxiv-2512-00589:
Cygnus X-2 is a bright X-ray binary where matter spirals from a star onto a neutron star. Misaki Mizumoto and co-authors present XRISM observations of its accretion disk corona in 2025. The high-resolution spectrum precisely characterizes iron emission lines from the corona.

The corona appears to have at least two distinct regions. The observations also suggest a possible ultra-fast outflow leaving the system. XRISM's sharp spectroscopy lets astronomers separate these components, refining the picture of how accreting neutron stars heat and expel the gas falling onto them. Z-sources are the brightest class of neutron star binaries, and Cyg X-2 is their prototype. Iron lines are the sharpest fingerprints in the X-ray band.
arxiv-2512-03089:
A safe off switch for a rogue AI agent is the idea here. Kai Williams, Rohan Subramani, and Francis Rhys Ward set out the plan in this 2025 work. Top AI firms may fail to align or control very strong agents, they note.

Their plan uses a password to trigger a safe shutdown. The agent is built so that, given the password, it stops in a set way. A clear stop rule could block harm in the real world. The work adds a fresh tool to talks on how to keep strong AI under human control. Safety teams could treat the password plan as one layer in a wider control system for future agents.
arxiv-2512-03289:
Music software gives control, but it can break a creative flow. Aaron Elkins and co-authors present DAWZY, an AI helper for music making, in this 2025 work. Turning a wish like warm the vocals into many small edits is slow in normal workstations.

Most AI music tools generate a whole track at once, leaving little room for the human. DAWZY turns text, voice, or hummed requests into reversible actions inside REAPER software. Users can undo steps and keep shaping the piece. The tool aims to keep people in charge of their music. Reversible edits respect the artist, since each AI action can be tried, judged, and undone in the session.
arxiv-2512-03389:
Data streams never stop, but language models usually answer once. Shu Chen, Deepti Raghavan, and Uğur Çetintemel bridge that gap in this 2025 work. Monitoring streams needs steady, meaning-aware computing over text that keeps arriving.

They introduce Continuous Prompts, a framework that brings model reasoning into stream processing. It is presented as the first of its kind for long-running analytics. Persistent prompts could watch news, logs, or sensor text for patterns as they form. That would extend AI help to live operations, not just one-off questions. Persistent processing suits alerts and dashboards, where questions stay open for weeks.
arxiv-2512-03489:
Sharp inequalities govern how functions spread on finite groups. Gan Yao proves optimal bounds of that kind in this 2025 work. The setting is cyclic groups whose sizes are powers of two, sometimes times three.

Yao studies a Poisson-like semigroup tied to word length on the group. He proves it is hypercontractive between the stated function spaces. He also addresses log-Sobolev inequalities, which control entropy decay. Optimal constants matter in probability, analysis, and theoretical computer science, where these tools are used daily. Word length geometry drives the semigroup, linking combinatorics to analytic bounds.
arxiv-2512-01889:
A robot or headset builds a map of its surroundings while tracking its own motion, a task called SLAM. A 2025 paper by Zaid Nasser and nine co-authors presents KM-ViPE, a real-time system that does this from a single ordinary camera, with no depth sensor and no advance calibration.

The system also labels what it sees in open vocabulary, meaning users can query objects by name rather than a fixed list. It works directly on raw video streams, even where the scene itself is moving. That makes it suited to head-worn, first-person applications and to learning from the huge supply of everyday internet video.
arxiv-2512-01989:
Physical AI aims at models that can perceive the real world and predict how it changes, a skill robots and vehicles depend on. Fengzhe Zhou and co-authors introduce PAI-Bench in 2025, a broad benchmark for measuring how well today's multimodal language models and video generators support that aim.

How far current models really grasp physical dynamics was poorly understood, because most benchmarks test words and pictures, not motion and cause. PAI-Bench evaluates models on their ability to perceive and forecast real-world behavior. The results give the field a shared yardstick for a capability that matters more as AI moves into physical settings.
arxiv-2512-02189:
NVIDIA's Blackwell generation of graphics processors adds fifth-generation tensor cores, a new tensor memory, and a dual-chip design aimed at machine learning and exascale computing. Aaron Jarmusch and Sunita Chandrasekaran microbenchmark the B200 architecture in 2025 to learn what these changes mean in practice.

Microbenchmarks poke one feature at a time, measuring exactly how fast each piece of hardware is rather than trusting headline numbers. The performance implications of the new architecture were poorly understood across diverse workloads. Careful measurements like these tell programmers how to write code that actually uses the silicon they paid for.
arxiv-2512-02289:
DocETL is an open-source system that runs language-model pipelines over messy, unstructured document collections, used in fields from journalism to law and medicine. Lindsey Wei and five co-authors extend it in 2025 with agentic rewrites that optimize these pipelines against several goals at once.

A year after release, the system had gathered thousands of users and GitHub stars across many domains. The new work lets an agent rewrite a data-processing pipeline and judge the rewrite on multiple objectives, like cost and accuracy together. Automated optimization of document pipelines could make large-scale text analysis cheaper and better at the same time.
arxiv-2512-02389:
Self-correction, noticing and fixing one's own mistakes, is something language models are usually taught by expensive reinforcement learning. David Wu and three co-authors test in 2025 a cheaper idea borrowed from driving and robotics: inject synthetic errors during supervised training and teach the model to recover.

Their title delivers the verdict: the trick fails to elicit genuine self-correction. Negative results of this clarity save a field from wandering down an attractive dead end. They also sharpen the question of what reinforcement learning provides that supervised exposure to mistakes does not, a question at the center of reasoning research.
arxiv-2512-02489:
Mithra D K takes on a hard health data problem: many measured traits, but few patients to learn from. Using NHANES survey data, the 2025 study tries to predict who has diabetes. Data shaped like this, with far more inputs than cases, can easily fool standard models.

The author first tests plain baselines, including logistic regression, random forest, and XGBoost. A hybrid model then pairs an XGBoost feature encoder with a small neural network head. Shrinking the input before the final step aims for steadier predictions, a useful pattern for clinics holding rich but small datasets. The same trick may help with heart, lung, or blood tests that share this shape of data.
arxiv-2512-02589:
Junyi Hou and four co-authors build an AI helper that lives inside the writing editor itself. Large language models already assist academic writing, but most tools sit outside the document. Cut off from structure and revision history, they cannot do deep, context aware work on a draft.

PaperDebugger is a plugin based multi agent system for editors such as Overleaf. Its agents review, edit, and polish text where the author actually writes. Help that sees the whole draft, and its past versions, could make AI feedback sharper and easier for scholars to accept or reject. Help that sits in the draft can flag a weak claim at the line where it first shows up.
arxiv-2512-02989:
Tommaso Tenna designs a relaxation scheme for flows moving through canal like networks. Hyperbolic conservation laws govern such flows, with physical conditions imposed where channels meet at a junction. Shallow water and blood flow equations both fit this network pattern.

The scheme approximates solutions without leaning on approximate Riemann solvers at each junction. A strategy drawn from earlier work handles the coupling cleanly. Robust network solvers help engineers model irrigation canals, flood channels, and blood vessel trees, where junction behavior decides the whole system's response. Joints are where net flows break ranks. A scheme that treats joints with care earns its keep on each run of a long canal or a heart tree.
plos-pone-0010189:
The authors were Jin Oshikawa, Norifumi Urao, Ha Won Kim, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study used mice to trace blood vessel growth after blocked flow. A signal protein, VEGF, drives new vessel growth, and its receptor needs reactive oxygen species to switch on fully. One key source is hydrogen peroxide made by an enzyme outside cells, called ecSOD.

The team showed that this peroxide promotes VEGF signaling inside tiny cell structures called caveolae. That signaling supported new vessel growth after ischemia, where blood flow was cut. The work may guide treatments that restore blood flow to damaged limbs.
plos-pone-0010289:
The authors were Paul Converse, Kathleen Eisenach, Sue Theus, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study questioned a lab habit in tuberculosis research. TB strains passaged many times in dishes may lose virulence, their power to cause disease. Some labs pass strains through mice first, hoping to restore that power before testing in mouse and guinea pig aerosol models.

The team measured the actual impact of mouse passaging before virulence testing. If passaging changes results, decades of comparisons between strains need re-reading. The study helps standardize how TB virulence is judged across laboratories.
plos-pone-0009789:
A new dinosaur from southern Utah adds a branch near the base of a famous family tree. Joseph Sertich and Mark Loewen described the fossil in PLOS ONE in 2010. The animal was a basal sauropodomorph, an early relative of the giant long-necked sauropods.

The bones came from the Lower Jurassic Navajo Sandstone. Basal means the species sits near the root of its group, before later specializations. Early members show what the group looked like before the giants evolved. Each new find sharpens the story of how sauropods began. Southern Utah keeps yielding important early dinosaur fossils.
plos-pone-0009889:
A sung word reaches the ear as both language and music at once. Reyna Gordon and colleagues asked whether the brain keeps those two streams apart. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Listeners heard words sung on different notes while their responses were timed.

Words and melody proved intertwined in perception, not processed in isolation. The team gathered EEG recordings, measures of the brain's electrical activity, plus behavioral evidence. Behavior showed the same blending that the brain signals did. The finding matters for how songs, speech, and music teaching work.
plos-pone-0009989:
Genes sometimes jump between species, and spotting those jumps in DNA takes special methods. Jennifer Becq, Cécile Churlaud, and Patrick Deschavanne benchmarked the main methods for that hunt. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

Horizontal transfer means a gene moves sideways between organisms, not down from parent to child. Parametric methods judge transfers from DNA composition clues. Such jumps can carry drug resistance between bacteria. A benchmark runs all methods on the same test so their scores can be compared. Honest scores tell genome scientists which method to trust.
